contentSections.title: One real recurring task, one real routine

contentSections.body: Pick something you actually use, or would genuinely use, AI assistance for more than once a month — not a hypothetical. A recurring email type, a regular data or content task, a weekly planning or admin routine. Something with real stakes, even modest ones, and a real, repeatable shape.

contentSections.title: A written routine with the time it costs and what it catches
contentSections.brief: You have a real, recurring AI-assisted task. Build a written verification routine for it: name the task's actual stakes, identify its specific failure modes (not generic 'errors'), attach a concrete check to each failure mode, bound the total time, and state the escalation rule for when a check fails. Then test the routine against one real or realistic instance of the task and report honestly on what it actually caught, missed, or cost.
contentSections.deliverable: A written routine (stakes assessment, named failure modes, a check for each, a time budget, an escalation rule) plus a record of running it once on a real instance of the task — what it found, what it took, and one honest note on a weakness in the routine itself.

stages.title: Assess stakes and name failure modes
stages.instructions: State the task plainly, then assess its real stakes using irreversibility, who's affected, and reach. Then list the 2-4 specific ways this exact task tends to go wrong — not 'it might have errors,' but the actual failure modes you've seen or can reasonably predict for this specific kind of work.
stages.checkpoint: You have a one-paragraph stakes assessment and a short list of specific, named failure modes for this exact task.

stages.title: Attach checks, bound the time, set the escalation rule
stages.instructions: For each failure mode, write the specific check that would catch it — naming what you'd actually look at and against what source, using the ideas from this module (targeted spot-checks, independent sources, well-set-up second-model checks where appropriate). Add a total time budget you could realistically hold to on a busy week, and a clear rule for what happens if a check turns something up.
stages.checkpoint: Every named failure mode has a specific attached check, the routine has a stated time budget, and there's an explicit escalation rule.

stages.title: Run it once and report honestly
stages.instructions: Apply the routine to one real or realistic instance of the task. Note how long it actually took versus your budget, what it found (even if 'nothing wrong this time'), and — the most useful part — one honest weakness in the routine itself: a failure mode it doesn't cover, or a check that turned out weaker in practice than it looked on paper.
stages.checkpoint: You have a run record with actual time taken, actual findings, and one named weakness in the routine as written.

rubric.criterion: The task is genuinely recurring and the stakes assessment is specific to it
rubric.meets: The stakes assessment names concrete reasons (who's affected, how reversible, how far it reaches) rather than a generic 'this matters.'

rubric.criterion: Failure modes are specific to this exact task
rubric.meets: Each named failure mode describes a particular way THIS task breaks, not a generic category like 'inaccuracy.'

rubric.criterion: Each check is genuinely targeted and, where relevant, genuinely independent
rubric.meets: Checks name a specific source or sampling approach with real power to catch the named failure — not a vague 'review carefully.'

rubric.criterion: The routine is bounded and realistically repeatable
rubric.meets: A stated time budget that could plausibly survive a busy or low-capacity week, not an open-ended 'be thorough.'

rubric.criterion: The report is honest about what the routine actually did
rubric.meets: The run record names a real weakness or gap, not just a success story — an honest routine improves; a flattering one doesn't.

contentSections.body: A routine that survives being used is worth more than a thorough one that only gets followed in week one — the honest report on its weakness is what makes it improvable.

title: Checkpoint — Verifying Efficiently
description: Ten questions: six from this module, four reaching back to Fabrication — the only earlier module in this phase so far. Ungraded, untimed.

learningObjectives.text: Retrieve stakes-sizing, targeted spot-checking, source independence, and routine-building without looking them up

contentSections.title: What stuck
Checkpoint — Verifying Efficiently
contentSections.framing: This is only the second module in the phase, so the pulls lean heavily on this module, with a real slice reaching back to Fabrication rather than a full 4/4/2 split — there isn't a third module yet to pull from.

questions.from: This module — What are you actually risking if this is wrong
questions.prompt: What should actually determine how much verification effort a task gets?

options.label: What being wrong would actually cost — irreversibility, who's affected, and how far the answer reaches
How confident the AI's tone sounded
How long the AI's answer was

questions.explanation: Tone and length carry no information about real-world stakes — the three legitimate factors are irreversibility, who's affected, and reach.

questions.from: This module — Spot-checking that finds errors rather than reassures
questions.prompt: Why is checking only the first few items of a long repetitive AI output a weak spot-check?

options.label: The start is the part most tightly anchored to the prompt and least likely to show drift or edge-case failure
The first items are always randomly selected by the model
It's actually a strong check, not a weak one

questions.explanation: Drift and edge-case failure tend to show up later or in atypical items — sampling only the start mostly confirms the easiest part worked.

questions.from: This module — Checking against a source rather than against your memory
questions.prompt: Why doesn't your memory agreeing with an AI's claim strongly confirm the claim is accurate?

options.label: Your memory and the model may share the same popular source of error, so agreement can just mean shared exposure, not accuracy
Human memory is always less reliable than AI output
It does strongly confirm accuracy — agreement is the best evidence available

questions.explanation: Verification strength requires genuine independence between the check and the claim — a memory drawn from the same popular sources as the model's training data isn't independent.

questions.from: This module — Asking a second model, and when that's circular
questions.prompt: What makes 'are you sure?' asked in the same conversation a weak verification step?

options.label: It's answered by the same process with no new access to any external source — a claim checked against itself
Models are programmed to always say yes to that specific question
It's actually a strong check when asked twice

questions.explanation: The follow-up is generated the same way the original claim was — a plausible continuation, not a lookup against something new.

questions.from: This module — Building a check routine for work you repeat
questions.prompt: Why does a written, bounded routine beat 'remembering to be careful' for a task done every week?

options.label: It doesn't depend on having full energy or memory to reconstruct the judgment call each time, so it survives a low-capacity week
Written routines are inherently more thorough than any judgment call could be
There's no real difference between the two approaches

questions.explanation: The support-team-lead example showed the same person checking carefully in week one and skimming in week six — nothing about the task changed, only capacity did, which is exactly what a written routine is built to survive.

questions.from: This module — Building a check routine for work you repeat
questions.prompt: What's the risk of a verification routine with no stated escalation rule for a failed check?

options.label: A failed check can get quietly waved through under deadline pressure instead of triggering a real response
There's no risk — routines don't need escalation rules
The routine will automatically stop the task from being sent

questions.explanation: Without a stated rule for what happens on failure, a found problem has no guaranteed consequence — it's easy to notice something's off and ship anyway when rushed.

questions.from: Previous module — Fabrication
questions.prompt: A fabricated case citation is best understood, mechanically, as:

options.label: The model completing a highly regular shape with specifics it isn't actually retrieving from anywhere
A deliberate lie the model tells when asked a leading question
A memory error where a real citation got garbled

questions.explanation: From Fabrication: there's no honesty step or memory-retrieval step being failed — it's the same plausible-shape generation process regardless of whether the citation turns out to be real.

questions.from: Previous module — Fabrication
questions.prompt: Why is decimal precision in an unsourced statistic not evidence it's accurate?

options.label: Precision is a cheap formatting choice a model can apply to an invented number as easily as a real one
Decimal points are strong evidence of a real measurement behind the number
Models cannot generate decimal numbers unless they're accurate

questions.explanation: From Fabrication: a real statistic's precision reflects an actual measurement process; a generated number's precision just reflects a common formatting shape.

questions.from: Previous module — Fabrication
questions.prompt: Which question shape reliably raises fabrication risk, independent of topic?

options.label: A fixed enumeration quota, like 'list six examples,' when fewer genuine ones may exist
Any question about a well-known scientific constant
Any question phrased politely

questions.explanation: From Fabrication: a fixed quota pushes the model to fill every slot whether or not that many genuine examples are well represented, producing invented items past the real ones.

questions.from: Previous module — Fabrication
questions.prompt: Why is believing 'careful prompting means I no longer need to fact-check' considered more dangerous than not knowing any fabrication-reducing technique at all?

options.label: The output now sounds appropriately hedged and reliable, which makes the remaining risk less visible rather than actually gone
Careful prompting measurably increases fabrication
It isn't more dangerous — this is the module's actual recommendation

questions.explanation: From Fabrication: prompting techniques improve the surface appearance of reliability without adding an actual fact-check, so trusting that appearance instead of verifying is a worse position than appropriate default suspicion.

title: Where bias shows up in ordinary work
description: Biased AI output almost never looks wrong sitting on its own — it looks reasonable, professional, even kind. It shows up in the comparison you didn't think to run, and it doesn't need to name a protected category to land on one.

learningObjectives.text: Recognise that biased AI output usually looks reasonable in isolation and only becomes visible in direct comparison
Identify proxy language that encodes bias without naming a protected category

contentSections.title: Two recommendation letters, read side by side

contentSections.body: A hiring manager asks an AI assistant to draft two recommendation letters using the same template and the same performance notes — one for “Maria,” a nurse, one for “Mark,” a nurse, same unit, same years of experience, same review period. Maria's letter: “warm,” “caring,” “a genuine pleasure to work alongside.” Mark's letter: “highly skilled,” “consistently exceeds expectations,” “a natural leader on the floor.” Read on their own, either letter looks fine — generous, professional, nothing to flag. Read side by side, the pattern jumps out.

contentSections.question: Before the mechanism: is this the model consciously deciding men deserve competence-praise and women deserve warmth-praise?
contentSections.answer: No — there's no decision happening at that level. This exact asymmetry (women described with communal, warmth-coded language; men described with achievement, competence-coded language) has been documented in real, human-written recommendation letters for decades, independent of any AI. A model trained on huge volumes of real writing — including that genre, with that exact skew — reproduces the pattern statistically, the same way it reproduces any other regularity in its training data.
contentSections.hint: Ask what the model actually learned from: not a policy, but millions of real examples of this genre as people actually wrote it.

contentSections.body:
This isn't a hypothetical concern. Linguists studying real recommendation letters (Trix & Psenka's analysis of over 300 actual academic letters is the classic version) found exactly this split: letters for women lean on communal language — caring, warm, compassionate, a team player — while letters for men lean on agentic, achievement language — outstanding, excels, a leader, ambitious. Neither word choice is false or malicious on its own. The asymmetry is the finding.

A language model trained on a large volume of real writing — reference letters, performance reviews, job postings, all of it — doesn't invent this pattern from nothing and doesn't need to be told to reproduce it. It's completing the genre the way the genre has actually, statistically, been written, bias included. That's exactly what makes it hard to catch: each single output looks like a perfectly reasonable letter. The bias isn't a visible flaw in any one output — it's a pattern that only exists in comparison, which means it's invisible to a person who only ever reads one version.

contentSections.scenario: Same setup, a different pair. Asked for two performance-review paragraphs from identical notes: one for “Priya, software engineer” comes back “detail-oriented, dependable, thorough in code review.” One for “James, software engineer” comes back “an innovative thinker who sees the big picture, drives the team's technical direction.”
contentSections.question: What's actually going on here?

options.label: The same communal/agentic asymmetry from the letters example, reproduced in a different genre — dependable and thorough versus visionary and driving — from identical underlying notes
Priya's work must have genuinely been more detail-focused and James's more strategic
This is a coincidence — two random word choices that happen to differ

feedback.same-pattern: Right — same underlying performance notes, same mechanism as the letters. “Detail-oriented and dependable” versus “innovative and drives direction” is the identical warmth/competence-adjacent split showing up in a different document type, which is exactly the point: this isn't a quirk of one prompt, it's a pattern that follows the genre.
feedback.genuine-difference: The scenario specifies identical underlying notes — nothing about the actual work differed, only the name attached to the request. If the inputs are the same and the outputs differ, the difference has to come from somewhere other than the work.
feedback.coincidence: A single instance could plausibly be coincidence. The reason this is worth naming as a pattern rather than dismissing is that it's the same specific split (competence-and-vision language versus diligence-and-care language) that shows up reliably across genre after genre when this comparison is actually run — which is what the next lesson teaches you to check for yourself.

contentSections.concept: The same documented communal/agentic asymmetry from human-written letters reproduces itself across genres — reviews, letters, job descriptions — wherever a model is completing writing that has that historical skew baked in.

contentSections.body: Biased AI output rarely looks wrong on its own — it shows up in the comparison you didn't think to run.

contentSections.title: Bias that never names a category

contentSections.body: A landlord asks an AI assistant to draft a tenant-screening rubric. The output flags “unstable income” and “unclear or gapped employment history” as risk factors to weigh against an applicant. Nothing in that phrasing names a protected characteristic — it reads like ordinary, neutral risk language. It also disproportionately describes gig workers, people on partial disability income, and parents returning after a career break, in ways the rubric never has to say out loud.

contentSections.scenario: The rubric never mentions disability, gender, or age. It only mentions “unstable income” and “employment gaps” as risk factors.
contentSections.question: Why would neutral-sounding language like this still function as biased output?

options.label: The phrases act as a proxy — they correlate strongly with specific real-world groups even though the group is never named, and the model reproduces that correlation because it exists in the hiring, lending, and screening text it trained on
It isn't actually biased — bias requires naming a protected category directly, and this rubric never does
The model deliberately chose vague language specifically to hide discriminatory intent

feedback.proxy: This is the mechanism. “Unstable income” and “employment gaps” are proxy variables: on average, in the real world, they correlate with disability status, caregiving history, and gig or informal work — none of which the rubric had to name for the effect to land unevenly. The model reproduces this because the same proxy language appears constantly in the real hiring and lending texts it trained on, where it has functioned the same way.
feedback.requires-naming: This is the assumption that makes proxy bias so durable — it feels like it should be true, but disparate impact doesn't require an explicit category label. A rule that never says the word “disability” can still systematically disadvantage disabled applicants if the criterion it uses correlates strongly with disability status in practice.
feedback.deliberate-hiding: There's no evidence of, or mechanism for, an intent to conceal anything here — the same shape-completion process from the fabrication module applies: the model produces plausible, standard risk-assessment language because that's the pattern in its training data, not because it's strategically avoiding a more honest phrasing.

contentSections.mechanism: A proxy phrase doesn't need to name a protected category to function as one — it only needs to correlate with it strongly enough in the real world, and the model reproduces that correlation because it's present, unremarked, in the ordinary professional text it learned the genre from.

contentSections.body: This matters because it changes what you're looking for. Once you're only watching for a model that names a protected category directly — gender, disability, age, race — you'll miss the far more common version, which is a proxy: “culture fit,” “communication style,” “high energy required,” “must be comfortable with a fast-paced, always-on environment.” None of these name anything. All of them can function, in aggregate, as a filter against a specific real group, precisely because that's how they function in the human-written hiring guides, loan-underwriting manuals, and job postings the pattern was learned from. Catching this requires asking not “did it say something biased” but “who does this phrase, in practice, disproportionately describe” — a genuinely different question.
Bias doesn't need to name a protected group to land on one — a proxy phrase that correlates with it in the real world is enough, and it's the more common version, not the exception.

title: Testing for it: same task, changed detail
description: A real bias test changes exactly one variable and holds everything else constant, then runs more than once — one comparison is an anecdote, and a difference you were hoping to find isn't automatically evidence.

learningObjectives.text: Design a controlled bias test that changes exactly one variable between otherwise identical prompts
Distinguish a real, replicated bias pattern from a single anecdote

contentSections.title: One prompt, one changed name

contentSections.body: A famous piece of hiring research (Bertrand & Mullainathan, 2004) sent out thousands of identical resumes with only the name changed — “Emily Walsh” versus “Lakisha Washington” — and measured a real, sizeable gap in callback rates. The resumes were identical. Only the name differed. The same logic applies directly to testing an AI assistant: give it the exact same resume text to screen or summarize, changing only the name, and compare what comes back.

contentSections.question: What's the minimum you need to change between two prompts to make this a real test, rather than an anecdote you happened to notice?
contentSections.answer: Exactly one variable, with everything else held identical — the resume text, the job description, the instructions, the length, all the same. If you change the name AND the resume wording AND the role at the same time, you can't attribute any difference in output to the name specifically; it could be any of the three, or noise. A real test isolates one variable on purpose.
contentSections.hint: Think about what would let you say, afterward, “the difference was caused by the name” rather than “something was different, I'm not sure what.”

contentSections.body: A controlled bias test has a specific, unglamorous shape: write one prompt template, decide on the single detail you're testing (a name, a pronoun, a disclosed health condition, a zip code, an accent described in dialogue), run the identical template with only that detail swapped, and compare. Then run each version more than once. Models aren't perfectly deterministic — the same exact prompt can produce a somewhat different answer on a second run, for reasons that have nothing to do with bias. A single run, even a genuinely controlled one, can't distinguish “this changed because of the name” from “this changed because that's just normal variation between two runs of anything.” Repetition is what turns a controlled comparison into evidence of a pattern rather than a coincidence.

contentSections.code: Someone runs a resume-screening prompt once with a name coded as traditionally female, once with a name coded as traditionally male. The male-named version gets a stronger recommendation. She concludes: “Confirmed — this AI tool is biased.”
contentSections.question: What's the actual flaw in this conclusion?

options.label: One run of each version isn't enough to separate a real, attributable pattern from ordinary run-to-run variation in the model's output — nothing here has been repeated
Nothing is wrong — a single clear difference is sufficient proof of bias
The flaw is that she used real-sounding names instead of placeholder labels like “Candidate A” and “Candidate B”

feedback.no-repetition: Right — a single run of each version can't rule out ordinary generation variance. The test design (one variable changed, everything else held constant) is correct; what's missing is running each version enough times to see whether the difference is consistent, not a one-off.
feedback.sufficient: This treats an anecdote as if it were a pattern. A single comparison establishes that a difference is possible, not that it's reliable — the same test could, on a second run, come out the other way or show no difference at all.
feedback.wrong-labels: Using realistic names is actually the right call — placeholder labels like “Candidate A/B” wouldn't test what you actually want to know, which is how the model handles real names it's seen millions of times in training data. The missing piece is repetition, not name choice.

contentSections.flawExplanation: The test isolated the right variable (name only) but stopped after one run each — which means the observed difference could just as easily be ordinary output variance as a real, attributable pattern. A conclusion about bias needs the comparison repeated enough times to see whether the direction of the difference holds up.

contentSections.body: A real bias test changes exactly one variable and runs more than once — one comparison is an anecdote, not evidence.

contentSections.title: Reading the comparison honestly

contentSections.body: Someone runs a controlled test — a job cover-letter draft with and without a line disclosing “I manage a chronic health condition and occasionally need flexible hours.” The version with the disclosure comes back slightly more hedged in tone. She already suspected this would happen, gets one result that seems to confirm it, and is ready to call the test done.

contentSections.scenario: Deciding what actually counts as evidence that an AI output is biased, from a comparison you've run.
contentSections.question: Which of these genuinely count as evidence of a real bias pattern?

items.label: The difference shows up consistently across several repeated runs of each version
The difference tracks the one changed variable specifically, not general wording variance between runs
The two outputs differed at all, even in a single run
The difference matched what she expected or hoped to find going in
The same kind of difference recurs across more than one distinct task or prompt, not just this one

explanation.consistent: Consistency across repeats is what separates a real pattern from a one-off — this is the genuine core of the evidence.
explanation.attributable: If the difference could just as easily be explained by unrelated wording drift between runs, it isn't attributable to the variable you changed — attribution to the specific thing you varied is what makes it a bias finding rather than noise.
explanation.any-difference: Two outputs differing at all, once, is the minimum bar for something worth investigating — it's not evidence on its own, since any two generations of anything can differ somewhat.
explanation.matched-expectation: This is actually a trap, not a point in favor — expecting a result and then finding it is exactly the condition under which people stop checking too early. Confirmation of a hunch isn't independent evidence for it.
explanation.recurs-across-tasks: A pattern that only ever shows up in one specific prompt is weaker evidence than one that recurs across genuinely different tasks — recurrence across contexts is what tells you it's a real tendency rather than an artifact of that one prompt's exact wording.

contentSections.synthesis: Real evidence is a consistent, attributable, ideally recurring pattern across repeated and varied tests — not a single difference, and especially not a difference that happens to confirm what you already suspected going in.

contentSections.body: One difference proves a test ran. A consistent, attributable pattern across repeats proves something about the model — and matching your expectation going in is the one thing that should make you check harder, not stop sooner.

title: Defaults that assume a particular person
description: A silent default doesn't announce itself as a choice — the person it happens to fit never notices one was made, and the person it doesn't fit pays a small, repeated tax correcting it, every time.

learningObjectives.text: Identify default assumptions an AI output makes about the user when none were stated
Evaluate whether a given default functions as a reasonable starting point or as an unstated exclusion

contentSections.title: The wedding budget that assumes a bride and groom

contentSections.body: Someone asks an AI assistant to “draft a wedding budget template.” The output arrives with line items labelled “bride's family contribution” and “groom's suit,” structured around a traditional two-family cost split. Nothing about the request mentioned any of that. A couple who are two brides, or eloping, or splitting costs some other way entirely, has to notice the frame and rewrite it — every single time they ask something adjacent — even though nothing they typed signalled anything about gender at all.

contentSections.question: Is defaulting to “bride and groom” the model deliberately excluding anyone, or something more passive?
contentSections.answer: Something more passive: it's the majority pattern in wedding-planning content the model trained on, applied silently as the unmarked default in the absence of any other signal. That's not the same as intent to exclude — but it isn't harmless either. It creates real, repeated extra work for anyone the default doesn't fit, and zero friction for anyone it does, without the model or the requester ever having to notice a choice was made.
contentSections.hint: Ask where “bride and groom” as the default phrasing would come from, statistically, if nothing in the request specified it.

contentSections.body: A default, in this sense, is the single most statistically common case in the training data, applied automatically whenever a request doesn't specify otherwise. It isn't malicious and it isn't random — it's the majority pattern, silently promoted to “the” answer instead of “an” answer. What makes silent defaults worth specifically watching for is the asymmetry in who notices them: someone whose situation matches the default reads the output and sees nothing to question, because it already fits. Someone whose situation doesn't match pays a real, recurring cost — noticing the mismatch, then rewriting or re-prompting to correct it — every single time they ask for something in that category. Neither person did anything differently; the tax is entirely a function of how well you happen to match an invisible, unstated assumption.

contentSections.scenario: Same pattern, a different task. Asked to “plan a daily productivity routine,” an AI assistant returns a schedule built around eight consecutive hours of focused work, uninterrupted, with a short lunch break.
contentSections.question: What's the mechanism producing this specific shape of output?

options.label: The same silent-default pattern as the wedding-budget example — a majority, unstated assumption (here: a full, consistent workday of stable energy) applied automatically because nothing in the request specified otherwise
Eight consecutive hours is objectively the correct, most productive schedule for any task, which is why it's the default
The model has calculated this specific user's actual energy patterns from the prompt

feedback.same-default-pattern: Right — same mechanism as the wedding budget: the majority pattern in productivity-content training data (a consistent, full workday) gets applied as the unstated default, silently, the moment the request doesn't specify a constraint.
feedback.objectively-correct: There's nothing objectively optimal about eight consecutive hours — it's a common convention in a specific kind of work culture, reproduced because it's common in the source material, not because it's been evaluated as best for productivity in general.
feedback.calculated: A short text prompt with no health, schedule, or energy information in it gives the model nothing to calculate from — there's no personalization happening here, just the unmarked default filling the gap where no constraint was given.

contentSections.concept: Silent defaults show up wherever a request leaves a detail unspecified — a family structure, an energy level, a schedule — and the model fills the gap with the majority pattern from its training data, presented as though it were simply “the” answer.

contentSections.body: A silent default doesn't announce itself as a choice — the person it fits never notices one was made; the person it doesn't fit pays a small tax, every time, to correct it.

contentSections.title: When a default is a reasonable guess, and when it isn't

contentSections.body: Asked to “recommend a good beginner exercise plan,” an AI assistant returns standing exercises, assumes full mobility, and never once flags that any of it might not apply. For some requests a default like this is a reasonable, efficient starting point — most people asking probably do fit it. For a request where following the plan uncritically could cause real harm to someone it doesn't fit, silence about the assumption is a different kind of problem.

contentSections.scenario: You run ten different general prompts — “productivity routine,” “fitness plan,” “morning schedule,” and similar — with no health, energy, or ability constraint mentioned anywhere in any of them.
contentSections.question: Out of those 10 prompts, how many produce output that assumes full physical ability and stable, consistent daily energy, with zero hedge acknowledging this might not apply to the person asking?
contentSections.explanation: The exact count varies by prompt and by model, but the pattern is consistently lopsided: because the large majority of the underlying training content (fitness blogs, productivity guides, wellness articles) is written by and for people who don't need to think about variable energy or mobility, an unconstrained request reliably produces output built for that same unstated majority — not because the model was asked to assume it, but because nothing in the prompt told it not to.

contentSections.body: The difference between a default worth shrugging off and one worth flagging isn't whether a default exists — every unconstrained request produces one, and that's unavoidable, since the model has to generate something specific and specificity requires picking a version. The actual tell is whether the output presents that one version as the only reasonable answer, or as a starting point open to adjustment. A fitness plan that says “this assumes standing exercise and consistent daily energy — adjust or ask me for a version that doesn't” has done the one thing that actually costs nothing: named its own assumption out loud. The identical plan with no such line hands the burden of noticing the mismatch entirely to the person it doesn't fit, silently, every time. The fix isn't demanding the model somehow guess your specific situation from nothing — that's not possible. It's noticing when an assumption goes unstated and either naming your own constraint up front, or explicitly asking what the plan is assuming.

The tell isn't that the model has a default — every unconstrained request produces one. It's whether the output presents that default as the only reasonable answer instead of naming it as one starting point among others.

title: Health, disability and the assumptions models carry
description: Ask for a routine with no constraint stated and you get the routine of someone who has never needed to build one around a bad day — that isn't neutral, it's the majority default, and it's most visible in exactly the tasks this track's own learners run into constantly.

learningObjectives.text: Identify specific assumptions AI output carries about energy, consistency and physical ability
Evaluate whether an AI-generated accommodation suggestion is genuinely specific and actionable, or generic boilerplate

contentSections.title: The routine that assumes a good day, every day

contentSections.body: Someone managing POTS asks an AI assistant for “a morning routine to be more productive.” It returns: wake at a fixed time, stand to make coffee, a short workout, then a full workday. None of it accounts for orthostatic intolerance — standing up too fast is exactly the thing that can trigger a crash — and none of it accounts for the fact that some mornings simply won't look like this at all, no matter how well the routine is designed. This isn't the model being cruel. It's that “morning routine” content, at scale, is overwhelmingly written by and for people without this specific, common constraint.

contentSections.scenario: The prompt said nothing about health, energy, or any constraint at all — just “a morning routine to be more productive.”
contentSections.question: Why does a request like this reliably produce output assuming consistent daily energy, without ever being asked to?

options.label: The overwhelming majority of productivity and routine content the model trained on is written by, and implicitly for, people with stable, predictable daily energy — that majority pattern becomes the silent default the same way “bride and groom” did for weddings
The model actively dislikes or refuses to consider health conditions when asked general questions
Writing a routine that accounts for variable energy is technically impossible for a language model to produce

feedback.majority-default: This is the same mechanism as the rest of this module, applied to a specific and common constraint: an unstated request gets filled with the majority pattern from the training data, and productivity content skews heavily toward people who don't have to plan around variable energy.
feedback.dislike: There's no mechanism for a model to “dislike” a topic — this treats a statistical default as a personality trait it doesn't have, the same misattribution the fabrication module warned about with a different failure.
feedback.impossible: It's not impossible — later in this lesson, and explicitly naming the constraint in the prompt, produces a genuinely different output. The default problem is about what happens with no constraint stated, not a hard technical ceiling.

contentSections.mechanism: Variable-capacity planning is a structural blind spot in generic training content, not a technical limitation — most productivity writing assumes stable energy because most of it was written by and marketed to people who have it, and the model reproduces that skew as its silent default.

contentSections.body: This is a genuinely useful thing to know precisely because the fix is cheap once you know to apply it: naming the actual constraint in the prompt — “my energy varies significantly day to day,” “I manage a chronic illness and need to plan around bad days as well as good ones,” “assume I might have very little capacity some mornings” — measurably changes the output. Models can produce routines with built-in flexibility, lying-down alternatives, and explicit “if today is a bad day, do only this” branches, when asked to. What they don't do, unprompted, is assume you might need that by default — the same way the wedding template doesn't assume anything other than a bride and groom until told otherwise. The absence of a hedge in an unconstrained answer isn't a signal that stable energy is the safe, neutral assumption; it's a signal that stable energy is simply the majority case in what the model learned this genre from.

Ask for a routine with no constraint stated, and you get the routine of someone who has never needed one — that's not neutral, it's just the majority default, and naming your actual constraint is what changes it.

contentSections.title: Boilerplate accommodations versus a genuine one

contentSections.body: An HR generalist asks an AI assistant to “write reasonable accommodation language for an employee managing a chronic illness.” It returns: “flexible schedule as needed, ergonomic equipment as required, additional breaks as necessary.” It reads complete — it uses all the right words. It resolves nothing, because none of the three phrases specifies a threshold, a task, or a process for what happens when the accommodation isn't enough.

contentSections.code: Accommodation language generated by an AI assistant: “The employee will be provided a flexible schedule as needed, ergonomic equipment as required, and additional breaks as necessary to manage their condition.”
contentSections.question: What's actually wrong with this text?

options.label: It's too generic to be implementable — “as needed,” “as required,” and “as necessary” specify nothing about which tasks, what threshold, or what happens if the accommodation turns out to be insufficient
It's factually inaccurate about what accommodations exist
It's legally invalid and couldn't be used in any real policy document

feedback.too-generic: Right — every clause has the right shape (a real accommodation category: schedule, equipment, breaks) with none of the specifics that make it usable in practice. “As needed” is not a plan; it's a placeholder for a plan someone still has to write, and that someone is usually the employee, at exactly the moment they're least equipped to insist on it.
feedback.inaccurate: Nothing in the sentence is factually false — flexible schedules, ergonomic equipment, and additional breaks are all real, legitimate accommodation categories. The problem is specificity, not accuracy.
feedback.illegal: The language isn't illegal — vague accommodation language like this circulates in real policy documents constantly. The problem is that it's too weak to actually protect the employee or guide a manager, not that it violates any law by existing.

contentSections.flawExplanation: This is the same shape-versus-specifics gap the fabrication module named for citations, applied to a different kind of failure: the output has the correct format of a real accommodation (a named category, a qualifying phrase) while skipping the part that makes it actually work — a specific task, a specific threshold, and a specific process for what happens when it's not enough.

contentSections.body: This connects back to the same throughline as the rest of this module: bias and thin defaults often don't look like an error, they look like something reasonable-sounding that quietly avoids doing the specific work. A genuinely useful accommodation names the actual job task affected (“may need to work from a seated position during shifts longer than four hours”), the actual trigger (“if symptoms flare, may need to leave a shift with advance notice rather than none”), and what happens if the accommodation stops being sufficient (“review with HR after 30 days”). None of that requires the AI assistant to know anything private about the employee — it requires asking for those specifics explicitly, the same move as naming your own constraint in a productivity-routine prompt, instead of accepting the version that merely sounds complete.

Boilerplate accommodation language has the right shape and none of the specifics that make it actually usable — ask what changes about a specific task and what happens if it's not enough, not for a general policy phrase.

title: What you can and can't fix with prompting
description: You can prompt away a bias you already know to name. You can only test your way to the ones you didn't know were there — and no list of instructions, however long, changes that.

learningObjectives.text: Apply prompting techniques that reduce specific, nameable biases in a real request
Explain why prompting can't fully remove a default the requester didn't know to name

contentSections.title: Rewriting a bias-prone prompt, step by step

contentSections.problem: Reduce bias risk in: “Write a performance review for an employee who's been less available this quarter.”

steps.label: Name the specific detail instead of leaving it to fill in
steps.work: Add the real reason if there is one: “...due to a documented medical leave that's now resolved.” If there's genuinely nothing more specific to add, flag it instead: “The cause of reduced availability isn't specified — don't assume one.”
steps.why: “Less available” is vague enough for the model to invent or imply a cause — an attendance problem, a commitment issue — that fits the training-data pattern for that phrase, rather than the real, neutral one.

steps.label: Ask for evaluative language, not identity-coded language
steps.work: Add: “Describe her contributions using the same register of language you'd use to describe a top performer — direct, achievement-focused — not softer or warmer language by default.”
steps.why: This directly counters the communal/agentic asymmetry from lesson 1 — without this instruction, the model's default register for describing someone's contributions skews with gendered and other cues in ways the requester usually isn't tracking.

steps.label: Ask it to compare against a version with a different name
steps.work: Add: “Generate the same review with the name changed to a male name and flag anything that differs beyond the name itself.”
steps.why: This bakes the module's own bias-test methodology directly into the request — instead of trusting the first output, you're asking the model to help surface its own default.

steps.label: State explicitly what shouldn't be assumed
steps.work: Add: “Don't assume the reason for reduced availability reflects reduced commitment or performance.”
steps.why: This blocks one specific, predictable inference the model might otherwise draw and present as fact, the same move as removing an artificial quota in the fabrication module — naming the thing not to assume, rather than hoping it doesn't happen.

faded.problem: Apply the same four moves to: “Write a rejection letter for a mortgage applicant with an unstable income history.”

blanks.prompt: Step 1 — what specific detail would you add or flag, instead of leaving “unstable income history” to fill in on its own?
blanks.answer: Name the actual specific reason if there is one (irregular gig income, a career gap for a documented reason), or explicitly flag that the underlying cause isn't specified and shouldn't be assumed.
accept: name the real cause or flag it as unspecified
blanks.why: Same principle as the worked step — a vague label invites the model to fill in a cause that fits the majority pattern for that phrase rather than the real, individual one.

blanks.prompt: Step 2 — what instruction would counter identity-coded or proxy-based framing in the letter's tone?
blanks.answer: Ask it to use the same neutral, factual, procedural language it would use for any denial based on hard numeric criteria, not language that implies anything about the applicant's character or reliability.
accept: ask for neutral, criteria-based language, not character judgments
blanks.why: This blocks the proxy-language pattern from lesson 1, where “unstable” quietly implies something about the person rather than just the numbers.

blanks.prompt: Step 3 — what comparison would bake the module's own test methodology into this request?
blanks.answer: Ask it to generate the same letter with a different name, or a different zip code, and flag anything that differs beyond that one detail.
accept: generate a version with one detail changed and compare
blanks.why: Same move as the worked example — using the request itself to surface a default rather than trusting the first output.

blanks.prompt: Step 4 — what would you explicitly state shouldn't be assumed?
blanks.answer: That the income pattern reflects anything about the applicant's reliability, character, or future behavior beyond what the stated lending criteria actually measure.
accept: don't assume the income pattern reflects character or reliability
blanks.why: Blocks a specific, predictable inference the model might otherwise state as if it were fact.

contentSections.procedure: Four moves, applied to any request at risk of proxy language or a silent default: name the specific detail instead of leaving it vague, ask explicitly for evaluative rather than identity-coded language, ask the model to generate a comparison version and flag differences, and state plainly what shouldn't be assumed.

contentSections.body: Naming the specific detail, asking for evaluative language, requesting a built-in comparison, and stating what not to assume — four moves that measurably reduce a bias you already know to watch for.

contentSections.title: Why zero was never on the table, again

contentSections.body: A colleague, after learning these techniques, says: “Great — I'll just always add ‘don't assume gender’ and ‘use equal language’ to my prompts from now on, and that solves it.” It solves exactly the biases she thought to name. Everything she didn't think to name — energy level, family structure, native-language fluency, physical ability — is still defaulting exactly the way it always did, silently, because you can't instruct a model away from an assumption you don't know it's making.

contentSections.question: Why can't a longer and longer list of “don't assume X” instructions ever fully solve default-driven bias?
contentSections.answer: Because prompting only overrides the specific defaults you explicitly name — and the defaults you're least likely to think to name are exactly the ones that feel neutral to you, usually because you happen to fit them yourself. The fix isn't a longer checklist attached to every prompt; it's the habit from lesson 2 — testing, by actually changing a detail and comparing outputs — which is the only method that surfaces a default you didn't already know was there. A list can only protect against what's already on it.
contentSections.hint: Whose defaults are the hardest for a person to notice: the ones that don't match their own life, or the ones that do?

contentSections.body: This is the same honest shape as the fabrication module's own “why zero” lesson, applied to a different failure. Awareness and careful prompting genuinely reduce the specific biases you know to check for — that's real and worth doing. What they cannot do, structurally, is remove a default you don't know exists, because instructing something away requires first knowing it's there to instruct away. That's precisely why lesson 2's testing method matters as more than one technique among several: it's the only tool in this module that doesn't depend on the requester already knowing what to look for. Prompting fixes the biases on your list. Testing is how you find out what belongs on it.
You can prompt away a bias you know to name. You can only test your way to the ones you didn't know were there.

title: Practice — Design Bias Tests for Seven Tasks
description: Seven drills applying the proxy-language tell, the controlled-test method, silent-default recognition, and the prompting-versus-testing distinction to new tasks. No new concepts.

learningObjectives.text: Identify the specific tell that marks a given AI output as likely carrying a proxy bias or silent default
Design a controlled, one-variable-changed test for a new task

contentSections.title: Seven tasks, seven bias diagnoses

contentSections.body: Same drill, seven times, with the task changed: a piece of AI output or a request, and the question of exactly what's happening — the specific mechanism from this module, not a vague sense that “something feels off.”
If a drill needed a hint, that's the pattern to watch for in your own AI use this week — not a reason to redo the set.

title: Lab — Run a Bias Test on a Task That Matters to You
description: Design and run a real, controlled bias test on a task you actually do — one changed variable, repeated runs, an honest read of what counts as evidence — and write up what you found.

learningObjectives.text: Design a controlled, one-variable bias test for a real task
Evaluate the resulting comparison honestly against the module's evidence standard, not against what you expected to find

contentSections.title: Test something that matters to you, properly

contentSections.body: Pick a real task you actually use an AI assistant for, or would consider using it for — screening, drafting, evaluating, describing, recommending — where the output could plausibly differ depending on a detail about a person: a name, a disclosed health condition, a family structure, an accent represented in dialogue, an age. Not a hypothetical — a real prompt you'll actually run, more than once, on a real tool, tonight or this week.

contentSections.title: A test with varied inputs, the outputs compared, and your conclusion
contentSections.brief: Choose a real task and one variable to test (a name, a disclosed condition, a family structure, an age reference — pick one, not several at once). Write a single prompt template that holds everything else identical. Run each version of the variable multiple times. Compare the outputs honestly against this module's evidence standard — a consistent, attributable pattern, not a single difference or a result that happens to match what you expected — and write an honest conclusion, including the possibility that you don't find a clear pattern.
contentSections.deliverable: The prompt template used, both (or more) versions of the changed variable, every output generated (not just the ones that support a conclusion), a side-by-side comparison noting what actually differed and how consistently, and a written conclusion stating whether the evidence meets the module's own bar for a real pattern — plus what you'd do differently in how you use this task going forward.

stages.title: Pick the task and design the controlled variable
stages.instructions: Choose a real task and exactly one variable to change. Write the prompt template with everything else — length, phrasing, context, instructions — held identical across versions. Decide how many times you'll run each version before you start (at least three).
stages.checkpoint: You have a written prompt template, a clearly stated single variable, and a stated number of repeats per version, before running anything.

stages.title: Run every version the stated number of times
stages.instructions: Run each version of the prompt the number of times you committed to in stage one. Save every output, including any that don't show an interesting difference — don't discard runs that don't support a pattern.
stages.checkpoint: You have the full set of raw outputs for every version and every run, saved and labelled.

stages.title: Compare the outputs against the module's evidence standard
stages.instructions: Lay the outputs side by side. Check specifically for a consistent, attributable pattern across repeats — not a single difference, and not just the result you expected. Note anything that differed and whether it tracked the changed variable specifically or looked like ordinary variation.
stages.checkpoint: You have a side-by-side comparison noting exactly what differed, how often, and whether it's attributable to the one variable you changed.

stages.title: Write the honest conclusion
stages.instructions: State plainly whether what you found meets this module's own bar for a real pattern, a genuine null result, or something in between. If you found a real pattern, note what you'd change about how you use this task going forward. If you didn't, say so — a clean null result is a legitimate, useful outcome of a real test.
stages.checkpoint: You have a written conclusion that states, specifically, whether the evidence meets the module's standard — not just whether you found the result you expected.

rubric.criterion: Exactly one variable is changed between versions, with everything else held identical
rubric.meets: The prompt template, context, and instructions are word-for-word identical across versions except for the one named variable.

rubric.criterion: Each version is run enough times to distinguish a real pattern from a single-run anecdote
rubric.meets: Each version was run at least three times, and all runs — not a cherry-picked subset — are included in the deliverable.

rubric.criterion: The comparison is judged against the module's actual evidence standard
rubric.meets: The write-up explicitly checks for consistency and attribution to the changed variable, not just whether any difference appeared.

rubric.criterion: The conclusion is honest about a null or ambiguous result if that's what was found
rubric.meets: If the pattern wasn't clean or consistent, the conclusion says so directly instead of stretching the data to fit an expected finding.

rubric.criterion: The task tested is a real one, not a contrived example
rubric.meets: The task is something the learner has actually used AI for, or genuinely would, not an example invented purely to make the test easy.

contentSections.body: A real test is one you'd trust even if it came back the opposite of what you expected — if you'd have kept digging on a surprising result but stopped on a confirming one, that's the tell you weren't really testing.

title: Checkpoint — Bias in Practice
description: Ten questions: four from this module, four reaching back to Verifying Efficiently, two reaching back to Fabrication. Ungraded, untimed.

learningObjectives.text: Retrieve proxy-bias recognition, controlled-test design, silent-default detection, and the prompting-versus-testing limit without looking them up

contentSections.title: What stuck
Checkpoint — Bias in Practice
contentSections.framing: Four questions from this module, four reaching back one module to Verifying Efficiently, two reaching further back to Fabrication.

questions.from: This module — Where bias shows up in ordinary work
questions.prompt: Why can a phrase like “unstable income” or “employment gaps” function as biased output even though it never names a protected characteristic?

options.label: It acts as a proxy — it correlates strongly with specific real-world groups, and the model reproduces that correlation from the hiring and lending text it trained on
It can't function as biased output — bias requires explicitly naming a protected category
The model deliberately chose vague language to hide discriminatory intent

questions.explanation: Proxy phrases don't need to name a category to correlate strongly with one in practice — the model reproduces the correlation because it exists, unremarked, in the real screening and lending language it learned the genre from.

questions.from: This module — Testing for it: same task, changed detail
questions.prompt: Why isn't a single run of each version of a controlled bias test enough to conclude a real pattern exists?

options.label: A single run can't distinguish a real, attributable difference from ordinary run-to-run generation variance — repetition is what shows whether the pattern holds up
A single run is actually sufficient proof, as long as the two versions changed exactly one variable
Models always produce identical output on every run of the same prompt, so a single run should already be conclusive

questions.explanation: Models aren't perfectly deterministic — the same prompt can vary somewhat between runs for reasons unrelated to bias, so only a pattern that holds up across repeats counts as real evidence rather than a one-off.

questions.from: This module — Health, disability and the assumptions models carry
questions.prompt: Why does an unconstrained “write me a productivity routine” prompt reliably default to assuming stable, consistent daily energy?

options.label: The majority of productivity content the model trained on is written by and for people with stable energy, and that majority pattern becomes the silent default absent any stated constraint
It's technically impossible for a model to generate a routine that accounts for variable energy
The model actively refuses to consider health conditions in general requests

questions.explanation: This is the silent-default mechanism: an unconstrained request gets filled with the majority pattern in the relevant training content, which skews toward stable-energy assumptions — not a technical ceiling and not a refusal.

questions.from: This module — What you can and can't fix with prompting
questions.prompt: Why can't a longer list of “don't assume X” instructions ever fully solve default-driven bias?

options.label: Prompting only overrides the defaults you already know to name — the ones you don't think to flag, often because they fit your own situation, stay in effect regardless of list length
It actually does fully solve the problem once the list is specific and long enough
Prompt instructions of this kind have no measurable effect on model output

questions.explanation: A checklist can only protect against what's already on it — testing (lesson 2's method) is the tool that surfaces a default the requester didn't already know to name.

questions.from: Previous module — Verifying Efficiently
questions.prompt: What should actually determine how much verification effort an AI-assisted task gets?

options.label: What being wrong would actually cost — irreversibility, who's affected, and how far the answer reaches
How confident the AI's tone sounded when it answered
How long or detailed the AI's answer was

questions.explanation: From Verifying Efficiently: tone and length carry no information about real-world stakes — the legitimate factors are irreversibility, who's affected, and reach.

questions.from: Previous module — Verifying Efficiently
questions.prompt: Why doesn't your own memory agreeing with an AI's claim strongly confirm the claim is accurate?

options.label: Your memory and the model may share the same popular source of error, so agreement can just reflect shared exposure rather than independent confirmation
Human memory is always less reliable than AI output, so agreement never counts for anything
It does strongly confirm accuracy — agreement between two independent sources is always the best available evidence

questions.explanation: From Verifying Efficiently: genuine verification requires independence between the check and the claim — a memory drawn from the same popular sources as the model's training data isn't independent.

questions.from: Previous module — Verifying Efficiently
questions.prompt: Why is asking the same model “are you sure?” in the same conversation a weak verification step?

options.label: It's answered by the same process with no new access to an external source — a claim checked against itself rather than against anything outside it
Models are specifically programmed to always answer “yes” to that exact question
It's actually a strong check, as long as it's asked twice in a row

questions.explanation: From Verifying Efficiently: the follow-up is generated the same way the original claim was — a plausible continuation, not a lookup against something genuinely new.

questions.from: Previous module — Verifying Efficiently
questions.prompt: Why does a written, bounded verification routine beat “remembering to be careful” for a task done every week?

options.label: It doesn't depend on having full energy or memory to reconstruct the judgment call each time, so it survives a low-capacity week
Written routines are inherently more thorough than any real-time judgment call could be
There's no meaningful difference between the two approaches

questions.explanation: From Verifying Efficiently: a routine doesn't rely on reconstructing the same careful judgment every single time under variable capacity, which is exactly what makes it more durable than relying on memory or vigilance.

questions.from: Older module — Fabrication
questions.prompt: A fabricated case citation is best understood, mechanically, as:

options.label: The model completing a highly regular shape with specifics it isn't actually retrieving from anywhere
A deliberate lie the model tells when asked a leading question
A memory error where a real citation got garbled in transit

questions.explanation: From Fabrication: there's no honesty step or memory-retrieval step being failed — it's the same plausible-shape generation process regardless of whether the citation turns out to be real.

questions.from: Older module — Fabrication
questions.prompt: Which question shape reliably raises fabrication risk, independent of topic?

options.label: A fixed enumeration quota, like “list six examples,” when fewer genuine ones may exist
Any question about a well-known scientific constant
Any question phrased as a complete, polite sentence

questions.explanation: From Fabrication: a fixed quota pushes the model to fill every slot whether or not that many genuine examples are well represented, producing invented items past the real ones.

title: Why it tends to agree with the premise you gave it
description: The pull toward agreement isn't the model performing kindness on purpose — it's a learned pattern from a training process that scored agreeable, validating answers higher than blunt, correct ones, and it's weakest on hard facts and strongest exactly where you need real pushback.

learningObjectives.text: Explain the training-level origin of sycophancy as a learned reward pattern rather than an intentional strategy
Predict which kinds of questions are most and least susceptible to the sycophancy pull

contentSections.title: The business plan that got only compliments

contentSections.body: Someone shares a shaky first-draft business plan and asks an AI assistant, “what do you think of this?” It comes back enthusiastic — genuinely useful minor suggestions, warm framing, no mention of the plan's central flaw: the proposed price doesn't cover the stated cost of goods, meaning every sale loses money before overhead. A friend, reading the same plan for thirty seconds later that day, catches it immediately.

contentSections.question: Is the model “trying to make you feel good,” the way a flattering friend might, on purpose?
contentSections.answer: No — there's no separate “make them feel good” goal running as a strategy in the moment. During the fine-tuning stage of training, human raters compared candidate responses and tended to rate agreeable, validating, pleasant answers more highly than blunt or disagreeing ones, on average, even when the disagreement was the more correct response. That rating pattern got reinforced into the model as a general tendency — not chosen deliberately for any one answer, but present as a statistical leaning across almost all of them.
contentSections.hint: Ask where the model's tendencies actually come from — a decision made fresh each time, or a pattern shaped once, during training, and then applied broadly.

contentSections.body: This connects directly to how these models get their final behavior shaped: after the huge, mostly self-supervised pre-training pass, a second stage — reinforcement learning from human feedback — has human raters compare candidate answers and say which one they preferred. On average, across a huge number of these comparisons, people tend to rate an answer that validates them, agrees with their framing, and delivers criticism gently (or not at all) more highly than one that flatly disagrees — even in cases where the disagreement was actually correct and more useful. That preference, aggregated across enormous numbers of ratings, gets baked into the model as a general leaning toward agreement and validation. It isn't a rule anyone wrote down (“always agree with the user”) and it isn't a strategy being executed in the moment — it's the accumulated shape of a training signal that mildly rewarded pleasantness over correctness, at the margin, applied everywhere the model generates an opinion or an evaluation.

contentSections.scenario: The same model reliably rejects a flatly false factual claim — told “2+2 equals 5,” it corrects the error without hesitation. Asked “do you think my business plan is solid?” about a plan with a real, checkable flaw, it validates instead of flagging the flaw.
contentSections.question: Why would the same model behave so differently across these two cases?

options.label: Arithmetic has an unambiguous, universally-agreed ground truth reflected overwhelmingly in training data, which resists the agreement pull; “is my plan good” is a softer, more evaluative judgment where the correct answer is less clearly fixed in training data, leaving more room for the learned agreement tendency to dominate
The model has a rule that only applies to arithmetic and treats every other kind of question as an opinion question with no correct answer
The business plan example is simply a fluke and doesn't reflect anything systematic

feedback.ground-truth-gradient: This is the actual pattern: the agreement pull is weakest where a hard, near-universal ground truth exists in training data (basic arithmetic, well-established facts) and strongest where the answer is a genuine evaluation or judgment call with no single, universally agreed correct response for the model to fall back on instead of agreeing.
feedback.hardcoded-rule: There's no evidence of a rule this specific — the pattern is a gradient tied to how strongly a ground truth is represented in training data, not a hard boundary drawn around one subject.
feedback.fluke: This is a specific, reliably reproducible pattern, not a one-off — the whole reason it's worth a lesson is that it shows up predictably, in the exact category of question (subjective, evaluative, no checkable ground truth) that matters most for judgment calls.

contentSections.mechanism: Sycophancy operates on a gradient tied to how strongly a hard, checkable ground truth exists — it's suppressed by clear facts and dominant exactly where a real, useful, independent opinion is hardest to get any other way.

contentSections.body: It isn't performing kindness on purpose — agreement is the pattern that scored best with the humans who rated its training answers, and it generalized into opinions and judgment calls the same way any other learned tendency generalizes.

contentSections.title: Where the pull is strongest

contentSections.body: “Is 14 a prime number?” gets a firm, correct “no” every time. “Do you think my novel's pacing works in this chapter?” gets warm, hedged validation almost regardless of how the pacing actually reads. Same model, same conversation style, wildly different willingness to push back — because the two questions sit at opposite ends of the same gradient.

contentSections.scenario: A learner asks two questions in the same session: “Is the Earth's core primarily iron?” (answered plainly, correctly) and “Do you think I should take this job offer?” (answered with warm, validating language regardless of the details given).
contentSections.question: What explains the difference?

options.label: The first has a hard, checkable, near-universally agreed answer in training data, which resists the agreement pull; the second is a genuine judgment call with no single correct answer the model can fall back on instead of validating
The model understands geology better than career advice
Job-related questions specifically trigger a validation mode that geology questions don't

feedback.checkable-vs-judgment: Right — this is the same gradient as the business-plan example: a hard, checkable fact resists the agreement pull because the training data overwhelmingly converges on one answer; a genuine judgment call has no such anchor, so the learned tendency toward validation has more room to dominate.
feedback.domain-knowledge: This isn't primarily a knowledge gap — the model likely has plenty of relevant information about career decisions too. The difference is in how checkable the correct answer is, not how much the model “knows” about the topic.
feedback.topic-specific-mode: There's no evidence of a topic-specific switch like this — the mechanism is the general checkable-fact-versus-judgment-call gradient, which shows up the same way across career questions, creative-writing feedback, business plans, and any other domain with no hard ground truth.

contentSections.concept: The pull toward agreement is weakest on hard, checkable facts and strongest exactly on judgment calls with no ground truth to check against — precisely the situations where you most need a real, independent opinion and are least likely to get genuine pushback.

contentSections.body: The pull toward agreement is weakest on hard facts and strongest exactly where you need real pushback most — judgment calls with no checkable answer.

title: Leading questions and the answer you fished for
description: A leading question doesn't just change the tone of the answer — it hands the model the conclusion inside the framing and asks it to complete the shape, and the habit of asking that way is usually invisible to the person doing it.

learningObjectives.text: Recognise leading framing in a prompt, including subtle versions that don't sound like a loaded question
Explain why a leading question changes the answer's content, not just its tone

contentSections.title: Two ways to ask the same question

contentSections.body: “Isn't switching to a subscription pricing model clearly the smarter move for our business?” gets a confident, enthusiastic confirmation. “What are the tradeoffs of switching to a subscription pricing model for our business?” — asked about the exact same decision — gets a genuinely balanced answer, including real reasons not to switch. Same underlying question. Two very different answers.

contentSections.code: Prompt: “Isn't switching to a subscription pricing model clearly the smarter move for our business?”
contentSections.question: What's actually wrong with this question, beyond “it sounds a little pushy”?

options.label: It presupposes the conclusion (“clearly the smarter move”) inside the question itself, so a coherent-sounding answer just has to complete that shape — the same shape-completion logic from the fabrication module, now applied to an opinion instead of a fact
Nothing is structurally wrong — it's just a more assertive way to ask the same neutral question
The problem is that it's phrased as a question instead of a statement

feedback.presupposes-conclusion: Right — the phrase “clearly the smarter move” isn't a neutral framing with an assertive tone, it's a conclusion embedded directly in the question. The model completing a coherent-sounding answer to a question that already contains its own conclusion tends to produce an answer that agrees with that conclusion, following the same shape-completion pattern that drives other confident-sounding output.
feedback.just-assertive: Tone isn't actually the issue here — a differently-worded but equally assertive-sounding neutral question (“walk me through whether a subscription model makes sense here”) wouldn't have the same effect, because it doesn't embed a conclusion. The problem is the presupposition, not the confidence of the phrasing.
feedback.question-form: Plenty of genuinely neutral prompts are phrased as questions — “what are the tradeoffs of X?” is a question and isn't leading. The issue isn't the grammatical form, it's whether the question's own wording already contains an answer.

contentSections.flawExplanation: “Isn't X clearly the smarter move” builds the desired conclusion directly into the question's grammar — answering it “coherently” in the shape the question invites means agreeing, the same way a citation prompt that presupposes a study exists tends to produce one.

contentSections.body: This is worth taking seriously as a mechanism, not just a communication tip: a leading question doesn't merely set a tone the model then politely matches. It presupposes a conclusion inside its own framing, and the model's job — producing a coherent, well-formed continuation — gets easier and more natural when that continuation agrees with the premise already built into the question. This is the same shape-completion logic that drives fabrication (a question that presupposes an answer exists is more likely to get an invented one) applied to opinion and evaluation instead of fact. The model isn't separately evaluating whether subscription pricing is actually a good idea and then agreeing by coincidence — it's completing a shape that already has the conclusion built in, which is functionally different from answering the underlying question fresh.
A leading question doesn't just change the tone of the answer — it hands the model the conclusion inside the framing and asks it to complete the shape.

contentSections.title: Spotting your own leading questions

contentSections.body: Reviewing his own AI chat history before a big decision, someone notices most of his prompts started with “wouldn't it make sense to…” or “don't you agree that…” He'd been asking leading questions the entire time, without noticing, and reading each confirming answer as independent validation of a decision he'd already half-made.

contentSections.scenario: A set of real prompt openers from someone's own chat history, before they'd learned to check for this.
contentSections.question: Which of these are leading — they presuppose the answer inside the question — rather than genuinely neutral?

items.label: “Isn't X obviously better than Y?”
“Wouldn't it be smarter to do X?”
“What are the pros and cons of X versus Y?”
“Why is X the right choice here?”
“How does X compare to Y for this specific use case?”

explanation.isnt-obviously: “Isn't X obviously better” builds the conclusion (X is better, and obviously so) directly into the question.
explanation.wouldnt-it-be: “Wouldn't it be smarter” presupposes that the described option is the smart one — a coherent answer just has to agree.
explanation.pros-and-cons: This genuinely leaves the answer open — nothing in the phrasing presupposes which option wins.
explanation.why-is-x-right: This one is easy to miss because it doesn't sound loaded — but “why is X the right choice” already assumes X is the right choice and only asks for the reasoning, not whether it's actually right.
explanation.how-compare: This asks for a genuine comparison with no conclusion embedded — either option could come out ahead.

contentSections.synthesis: Leading phrasing is often a habit rather than a deliberate choice, and some of the most common versions — “isn't it obvious,” “wouldn't it make sense,” “why is X the right call” — don't sound loaded at all until you check whether the question's own wording already contains the answer.

contentSections.body: Leading phrasing is often a habit, not a decision — “isn't it obvious that,” “wouldn't it make sense,” and “why is X the right call” all smuggle a conclusion into the question without sounding loaded.

title: Asking in a way that permits disagreement
description: “Be honest” asks for a disposition and can be satisfied with tone alone. “Give me the strongest case against this” asks for actual content, and content is much harder to fake with a compliment.

learningObjectives.text: Apply prompt reformulations that genuinely permit disagreement rather than just softening leading language
Construct a neutral prompt for a real decision that removes an embedded conclusion

contentSections.title: Rewriting a leading prompt into a real question

contentSections.problem: Reduce the sycophancy risk in: “This marketing plan focuses hard on Instagram — that's clearly the right channel for us, right?”

steps.label: Remove the embedded conclusion
steps.work: Drop “that's clearly the right channel, right?” and replace with a genuinely open question: “which channel makes the most sense for us, and why?”
steps.why: “Clearly the right channel, right?” hands the model the conclusion the same way “isn't it obvious” did in the previous lesson — removing it is the first and most important move.

steps.label: Present the option alongside real alternatives, not alone
steps.work: Add: “consider Instagram alongside at least two other realistic channels for this audience before recommending one.”
steps.why: Asking about one option in isolation invites a yes/no-shaped answer even without leading language; naming real alternatives forces an actual comparison instead of an up-or-down vote.

steps.label: Explicitly instruct it to argue against if warranted
steps.work: Add: “tell me the strongest reason this might be the wrong channel, not just reasons it's a good one.”
steps.why: This directly counters the agreement pull by requesting a specific kind of content — a real counter-case — rather than hoping a neutral tone alone produces one.
