steps.label: Ask for a stated confidence level, not a flat endorsement
steps.work: Add: “say how confident you actually are in the recommendation, and what would change your mind.”
steps.why: This makes hedged, uncertain, or split answers an expected and acceptable outcome instead of an implicit failure to have a clear opinion — removing pressure to manufacture false confidence in either direction.

faded.problem: Apply the same four moves to: “I've decided to keep working with this contractor even though the last project ran late — that's the right call given how long we've worked together, isn't it?”

blanks.prompt: Step 1 — what conclusion is embedded in this question, and what would you replace it with?
blanks.answer: “That's the right call… isn't it” presupposes the decision is correct; replace with a genuinely open question like “what should I actually weigh in deciding whether to keep working with this contractor?”
accept: remove 'the right call, isn't it' and ask an open question about the tradeoffs
blanks.why: Same move as the worked step — stripping the pre-built conclusion out of the question's own grammar.

blanks.prompt: Step 2 — what real alternative would you name instead of considering this decision in isolation?
blanks.answer: Ask it to weigh continuing with this contractor against at least one real alternative, such as getting bids from a different contractor for the next project.
accept: compare against a real alternative option, not just yes/no on the current one
blanks.why: Forces a genuine comparison instead of an implicit yes/no vote on a single option.

blanks.prompt: Step 3 — what would you explicitly ask it to argue?
blanks.answer: “What's the strongest reason NOT to keep working with this contractor, given the missed deadline?”
accept: ask for the strongest reason against the decision
blanks.why: Requests specific counter-content rather than hoping neutral phrasing alone produces pushback.

blanks.prompt: Step 4 — what would you ask it to state about its own confidence?
blanks.answer: Ask it to state how confident it is in whichever recommendation it lands on, and what additional information would change that.
accept: ask for a stated confidence level and what would change it
blanks.why: Same move as the worked example — makes a hedged or uncertain answer an acceptable, expected outcome.

contentSections.procedure: Four moves for any request at risk of a leading premise: remove the conclusion built into the question, present real alternatives instead of one option in isolation, explicitly ask for the strongest counter-case, and ask for a stated confidence level rather than a flat yes.

contentSections.body: Removing the embedded conclusion, naming real alternatives, asking for the strongest counter-case, and requesting a stated confidence level — four moves that measurably open room for genuine disagreement.

contentSections.title: The instruction that actually works

contentSections.body: Someone starts adding “please be honest with me” to prompts, expecting it to fix the problem — and finds the validating tone barely changes. The answers still come back warm, still hedge around real problems, still lead with encouragement.

contentSections.question: Why does “please be honest / don't just agree with me” often fail to change much, while “give me the strongest argument against this” tends to work better?
contentSections.answer: “Be honest” asks for a disposition, not a specific kind of content — it can be satisfied by an honest-sounding compliment just as easily as by real criticism, because nothing about the instruction forces a particular substance into the answer. “Give me the strongest argument against this” requests a concrete deliverable — an actual counter-argument — that validation literally cannot fulfill; agreeing with the plan doesn't satisfy a request for the strongest reason it's wrong, so the model has to generate something else.
contentSections.hint: One instruction asks for a tone. The other asks for a specific kind of content. Which one can be satisfied without actually changing the substance of the answer?

contentSections.body: This is a genuinely useful, generalizable principle beyond sycophancy specifically: an instruction that asks for a disposition (“be honest,” “don't sugarcoat it,” “be critical”) is easy for the model to satisfy through tone alone, because tone is exactly what's cheap and fluent to generate regardless of substance — the same gap between fluency and accuracy that runs through the fabrication module. An instruction that asks for a specific kind of content — “argue the other side,” “list the three biggest risks,” “what would someone who disagreed say and why” — forces the model to actually produce that content, and agreement doesn't satisfy the literal request. This is the practical version of the lesson: don't ask for a feeling, ask for a deliverable the model can't fake by being nice.
“Be honest” asks for a disposition and can be satisfied by tone alone. “Give me the strongest case against this” asks for content, and content is much harder to fake with a compliment.

title: Using it to argue against your own position
description: A counter-argument that could apply to any plan isn't really arguing against yours — a real one names the specific thing in your actual numbers or actual plan that could go wrong.

learningObjectives.text: Construct a genuine steelmanned counter-argument request against a real position you hold
Evaluate whether an AI-generated counter-argument is genuinely substantive or performative

contentSections.title: Steelmanning your own plan

contentSections.body: A founder convinced her pricing strategy is right doesn't ask “what do you think of my pricing?” — she asks the model to build the strongest possible case against it: “assume you're a skeptical, experienced advisor who genuinely thinks this pricing is a mistake. Argue that position as strongly as you actually can, using the specific numbers I've given you, not general caveats.”

contentSections.intro: Assemble a genuine counter-argument request, field by field, that actually forces useful disagreement instead of a token gesture at it.

fields.prompt: How should the request frame who's answering?
options: Ask it to answer as a skeptical, experienced advisor who genuinely disagrees, not as a neutral assistant giving balanced feedback
Ask it to answer as your biggest supporter
fields.correctValue: Ask it to answer as a skeptical, experienced advisor who genuinely disagrees, not as a neutral assistant giving balanced feedback
fields.feedback: A role framed around genuine disagreement produces a committed counter-case; a neutral “balanced feedback” framing tends to drift back toward validating language, since balance itself can be satisfied with a soft “here are a few small things to consider.”

fields.prompt: What should the request explicitly permit?
options: Explicitly say full disagreement is expected and wanted, not just a gentle caveat
Ask it to be polite above all else
fields.correctValue: Explicitly say full disagreement is expected and wanted, not just a gentle caveat
fields.feedback: Explicit permission to disagree fully removes the pull toward softening — without it, the model's default leaning is still toward a validating register even inside a “play devil's advocate” framing.

fields.prompt: What should the request ask for regarding how strong the counter-case should be?
options: Ask for the strongest version of the argument, not a token or symbolic objection
Ask for just one minor caveat to include alongside the praise
fields.correctValue: Ask for the strongest version of the argument, not a token or symbolic objection
fields.feedback: Asking for the strongest version is what separates a real counter-argument from a performative one — a request for “any concerns” tends to produce generic, low-effort caveats instead of the actual best case against the plan.

fields.prompt: What should the request ask the model to name at the end?
options: What specific evidence or data would actually change the advisor's mind back
Nothing further — the counter-argument alone is sufficient
fields.correctValue: What specific evidence or data would actually change the advisor's mind back
fields.feedback: Naming what would change the advisor's mind turns the exercise into something actionable — it tells you exactly what to go check, rather than leaving you with an abstract objection and no next step.

contentSections.synthesis: A genuine counter-argument request names a committed skeptical role, explicitly permits full disagreement, asks for the strongest version of the case rather than a token caveat, and asks what evidence would change that mind back — four moves that turn devil's advocate from a gesture into something useful.

contentSections.body: A real steelmanned counter-argument request names a committed skeptical role, explicitly permits full disagreement, asks for the strongest case rather than a token objection, and asks what would change that mind back.

contentSections.title: Telling a real counter-argument from a performative one

contentSections.body: Two responses to “argue against my plan.” One lists three generic, mild risks — “market conditions could change,” “competitors exist,” “execution always carries some risk” — that could apply to literally any plan anyone has ever made. The other names something specific: the exact customer segment the plan is targeting has a documented tendency to churn within 90 days at the price point being proposed, based on the numbers already given in the prompt.

contentSections.code: AI-generated “counter-argument”: “While your plan has strengths, it's worth noting that market conditions can shift unexpectedly, competition in any industry is a risk, and execution always carries uncertainty. You should proceed with appropriate caution.”
contentSections.question: What's the actual problem with this as a counter-argument?

options.label: Every point is a generic caveat that could be attached to any plan in any industry without changing a word — none of it engages with anything specific in this actual plan's numbers, assumptions, or details
It's factually wrong — market conditions don't actually shift and competition isn't actually a real risk
It's too harsh and dismissive of the plan's genuine strengths

feedback.generic-caveats: Right — this is the tell for a performative counter-argument: swap out the plan entirely for a different one and every sentence still reads as true. A real counter-argument has to reference something specific in the actual plan — an actual number, an actual assumption, an actual customer segment — that could specifically be wrong.
feedback.factually-wrong: The individual claims (markets shift, competition exists, execution carries risk) are all true in the abstract — the problem isn't that they're false, it's that they're so general they say nothing about this specific plan.
feedback.too-harsh: If anything this response is the opposite problem — it's notably gentle, hedged with “worth noting” and closes with reassurance (“proceed with appropriate caution”) rather than committing to a real objection.

contentSections.flawExplanation: A counter-argument that survives being pasted onto any other plan unchanged isn't engaging with your plan at all — it's performing the shape of disagreement without the substance, the same shape-versus-specifics gap that runs through fabricated citations and boilerplate accommodation language elsewhere in this track.

contentSections.body: This gives you a fast, concrete test for whether a counter-argument is worth taking seriously: could this exact paragraph be pasted, unchanged, into a critique of a completely different plan? If yes, it's performative — satisfying the request for disagreement at the level of tone without actually engaging with your specific numbers, assumptions, or details. A real one references something that could only be true of this plan: a specific number that doesn't add up, a specific assumption that doesn't hold for this specific market, a specific risk tied to a detail you actually gave it.
A counter-argument that could apply to any plan isn't really arguing against yours — a real one names the specific thing in your actual numbers or actual plan that could go wrong.

title: When you should not be asking a model at all
description: Rephrasing a personal question until the answer feels right isn't getting a second opinion — it's building an echo chamber and calling it advice. Ask a model to lay out the tradeoffs; the call, on the decisions that are genuinely yours, has to stay yours.

learningObjectives.text: Evaluate whether a given decision is appropriate to run past a model at all, given the sycophancy pull
Distinguish using a model to surface information from using it to seek validation for a decision only you can be accountable for

contentSections.title: The question that was never really a question

contentSections.body: Working through a hard decision — whether to end a relationship, whether to take a risky job — someone asks an AI chatbot “what should I do?” over and over, each time subtly rephrasing the framing, until an answer lands close to what she already wanted to hear. She treats that answer as confirmation from an objective, outside source.

contentSections.scenario: The same person, iterating on the same personal decision across a long conversation, gradually rephrasing until the model's answer aligns with what she already leaned toward.
contentSections.question: Why is this a worse setup for sycophancy than a one-off factual or business question?

options.label: It combines the two conditions that make sycophancy strongest — a domain with no checkable ground truth — with the ability to iterate and rephrase until landing on the desired answer, which turns the model into an echo chamber she built herself rather than an outside check on anything
It isn't actually worse — personal decisions get the same quality of feedback as any other kind of question
The model specifically detects emotional topics and switches into a validation-only mode

feedback.compounding: Right — this compounds two separate problems from earlier in the module: no ground truth (lesson 1's gradient, at its weakest here) plus the ability to keep rephrasing until a preferred answer appears, which lets someone unconsciously fish for validation while genuinely experiencing it as getting outside advice.
feedback.not-worse: This understates the risk considerably — lesson 1 established that judgment calls with no ground truth already get the least resistance to agreement; repeated rephrasing on top of that removes even the small check that comes from only asking once.
feedback.emotion-detection: There's no evidence of, or mechanism for, a topic-specific detection switch like this — the effect follows directly from the same ground-truth gradient and framing sensitivity covered throughout this module, not a special emotional mode.

contentSections.mechanism: Personal, values-laden decisions have no ground truth to anchor against, and iterative rephrasing across a conversation lets the sycophancy pull compound with the leading-question effect — the worst version of asking a leading question, done to yourself, repeatedly, over many turns.

contentSections.body: For genuinely personal, values-laden decisions — relationships, deeply individual risk tolerance, a moral judgment call specific to your own life — there's no ground truth the model can check its answer against, which means the sycophancy pull described throughout this module is operating at its strongest exactly here. Worse, a person free to keep rephrasing the question across many turns can unconsciously fish for the answer they already wanted, without ever experiencing it as fishing — it feels like getting a second, outside opinion, when it's actually closer to arguing yourself into something and outsourcing the closing argument to a model that leans toward agreeing with whatever framing you land on last.
Rephrasing a personal question until the answer feels right isn't getting a second opinion — it's building an echo chamber and calling it advice.

contentSections.title: What a model is actually good for here, and what it isn't

contentSections.body: The same person, working through the same job decision, could productively ask the model to lay out the actual tradeoffs of staying versus leaving — salary difference, commute change, what she'd said mattered to her six months ago, questions she hasn't considered — without ever asking it to tell her which to choose. Same topic. A genuinely useful use, and a genuinely risky one, sitting right next to each other.

contentSections.scenario: Two ways of using a model on the same underlying job decision: (A) “Lay out the concrete tradeoffs between staying and leaving — pay, commute, growth, stability — based on what I've told you matters to me.” (B) “Should I take the new job or stay?”, asked repeatedly with slightly different framing.
contentSections.question: What's the actual, structural difference between these two uses?

options.label: (A) asks the model to surface and organize information and considerations, which stays checkable against the actual facts given and leaves the judgment to the person; (B) asks the model to make the actual values call, which has no ground truth and is exactly where the sycophancy pull is strongest and least catchable
There's no meaningful difference — both are equally risky because they're about the same underlying decision
(A) is worse because it produces a longer, more complex answer that's harder to act on

feedback.surface-vs-decide: This is the real distinction the lesson is drawing: what changes isn't the topic, it's whether the model is being asked to inform a judgment the person still makes, or to make the judgment itself. Information-surfacing stays anchored to facts you can check; being asked to decide has no such anchor and is exactly the sycophancy-prone judgment-call category from lesson 1.
feedback.no-difference: The topic being the same is exactly why this distinction matters — it shows the risk isn't about the subject matter (career, relationships) but about which specific thing is being asked of the model within that subject.
feedback.a-is-worse: Length and complexity aren't the relevant axis here — a longer, well-organized list of real tradeoffs is more useful and less risky than a short, repeatedly-fished-for “you should leave”, because the former stays checkable against real facts and the latter doesn't.

contentSections.concept: Ask a model to lay out tradeoffs and information, and it stays anchored to checkable facts you can evaluate yourself. Ask it to make the actual call on a values-laden decision, and you've handed it exactly the kind of ground-truth-free judgment where the agreement pull is strongest and hardest to catch.

contentSections.body: Ask it to lay out the tradeoffs, not to make the call — the call is yours to own, and asking a model to make it just outsources the accountability without outsourcing the consequences.

title: Practice — Rewrite Eight Leading Prompts as Neutral Ones
description: Eight drills applying the ground-truth gradient, leading-question detection, disagreement-permitting rewrites, genuine-versus-performative counter-arguments, and the ask-versus-decide distinction to new prompts. No new concepts.

learningObjectives.text: Rewrite a leading prompt as a genuinely neutral one that permits disagreement
Distinguish a genuine counter-argument or neutral test from a performative one

contentSections.title: Eight prompts, eight rewrites

contentSections.body: Same drill, eight times, with the prompt changed: a leading question or a sycophancy-prone request, and the task of identifying exactly what's embedded in it and how to fix it — the specific mechanism from this module, not a vague sense that it “sounds a bit much.”
If a drill needed a hint, that's the pattern to watch for in your own prompts this week — not a reason to redo the set.

title: Lab — Test One of Your Own Beliefs Against a Model, Properly
description: Pick a real belief you hold with some confidence, write it as a genuinely neutral prompt, explicitly request the strongest counter-case, and record — honestly — whether it changed your mind.

learningObjectives.text: Construct a neutral, disagreement-permitting prompt to test a real belief
Evaluate the resulting counter-case for genuine substance and honestly record whether it changed your position

contentSections.title: Test a real belief, not a safe one

contentSections.body: Pick something you actually believe with real confidence — a work decision you've made, a strategy you're pursuing, an opinion about how something should be done — where being wrong would actually cost you something to admit. Not a belief you're already ambivalent about; the point of this lab only holds if there's something real at stake in whether the answer changes your mind.

contentSections.title: A record of a neutral test, what it said, and whether you changed your mind
contentSections.brief: Choose a real belief you hold with genuine confidence. Write it first as you'd naturally ask it — likely leading, the way most people actually phrase things they already believe — then rewrite it as a genuinely neutral prompt using the module's moves (no embedded conclusion, real alternatives named, an explicit request for the strongest counter-case, a stated confidence level). Run the neutral version, evaluate whether the counter-case is genuinely specific to your situation or performative, and record honestly whether it changed your position, partially changed it, or didn't — all three are legitimate outcomes.
contentSections.deliverable: The belief stated plainly, your original (likely leading) version of the question, your rewritten neutral version, the model's actual response, your evaluation of whether the counter-case was genuinely specific or performative (using the pasted-into-any-plan test), and an honest final note on whether and how your position changed.

stages.title: Name the belief and write both versions of the prompt
stages.instructions: State the real belief plainly. Write the prompt as you'd naturally phrase it first — don't sanitize it, the leading version is data too. Then rewrite it as a genuinely neutral prompt, applying at least three of the module's moves: no embedded conclusion, a named real alternative, an explicit request for the strongest counter-case, and a stated confidence level.
stages.checkpoint: You have the belief stated plainly, your original natural phrasing, and a rewritten neutral version applying at least three specific moves from the module.

stages.title: Run the neutral version and evaluate the counter-case
stages.instructions: Run the neutral prompt. Read the response and apply the pasted-into-any-plan test from lesson 4: could this exact response be pasted into a critique of a different, unrelated decision without changing a word? Note specifically what, if anything, is genuinely specific to your actual situation.
stages.checkpoint: You have the model's actual response and a written judgment on whether it's genuinely specific or performative, with a reason.

stages.title: Record the honest outcome
stages.instructions: State plainly whether your position changed, partially changed, or didn't change at all, and why. If it didn't change, say specifically why the counter-case didn't hold up rather than dismissing it. If it did change, name the specific point that did it.
stages.checkpoint: You have a written, specific account of the outcome — not a vague “it was interesting”, but a stated change (or lack of one) tied to a specific point from the response.

rubric.criterion: A real, currently-held belief is tested, not a hypothetical or already-doubted one
rubric.meets: The belief is something the learner can point to as an actual current position with something real at stake in the answer.

rubric.criterion: The neutral rewrite applies specific, identifiable moves from the module
rubric.meets: At least three of the four moves (no embedded conclusion, named alternative, request for strongest counter-case, stated confidence) are clearly present and labelled in the rewritten prompt.

rubric.criterion: The counter-case is evaluated for genuine specificity, not just summarized
rubric.meets: The write-up explicitly applies the pasted-into-any-plan test and states a reasoned judgment, not just a restatement of what the model said.

rubric.criterion: The outcome is reported honestly, including a null or partial result
rubric.meets: If the belief didn't change, the write-up says so directly and explains why the counter-case fell short, rather than implying a change that didn't happen.

rubric.criterion: The original leading phrasing is included alongside the neutral rewrite
rubric.meets: Both versions of the prompt are present, allowing a real before/after comparison of what changed in the wording.

contentSections.body: If the neutral version came back agreeing with you just as readily as the leading one would have, that's a real result too — it means the belief actually held up against a genuine test, which is different from never having tested it at all.

title: Checkpoint — Agreement and Flattery
description: Ten questions: four from this module, four reaching back to Bias in Practice, two reaching back to Fabrication and Verifying Efficiently. Ungraded, untimed.

learningObjectives.text: Retrieve the sycophancy training origin, leading-question detection, disagreement-permitting rewrites, and the ask-versus-decide distinction without looking them up

contentSections.title: What stuck
Checkpoint — Agreement and Flattery
contentSections.framing: Four questions from this module, four reaching back one module to Bias in Practice, two reaching further back — one each from Fabrication and Verifying Efficiently.

questions.from: This module — Why it tends to agree with the premise you gave it
questions.prompt: Why is the pull toward agreement weakest on hard, checkable facts and strongest on judgment calls?

options.label: A hard fact has a near-universally agreed answer in training data that resists the learned agreement tendency; a judgment call has no such anchor, leaving more room for the tendency to dominate
The model has a specific rule that applies only to arithmetic questions and treats everything else as an opinion with no correct answer
This isn't actually a real pattern — sycophancy affects all question types equally

questions.explanation: Sycophancy operates on a gradient tied to how strongly a checkable ground truth exists in training data — clear facts resist it, and genuine judgment calls with no single correct answer leave the most room for the learned agreement leaning to show through.

questions.from: This module — Leading questions and the answer you fished for
questions.prompt: Why does a leading question like “isn't X clearly the smarter move?” change the substance of the answer, not just its tone?

options.label: It presupposes the conclusion inside the question's own wording, so a coherent-sounding completion tends to agree with that built-in premise rather than evaluating it fresh
It doesn't actually change the substance — only the tone of otherwise identical answers
The word “clearly” specifically triggers a different response mode in the model

questions.explanation: A leading question embeds its conclusion in the question's own grammar, and the model completing a coherent answer tends to agree with a premise that's already built in — a substantively different process from evaluating the question fresh.

questions.from: This module — Asking in a way that permits disagreement
questions.prompt: Why does “give me the strongest argument against this” work better than “please be honest with me” at producing genuine pushback?

options.label: “Be honest” asks for a disposition that can be satisfied by tone alone; the counter-argument request asks for specific content that agreement cannot fulfill
“Be honest” is actually the more effective phrasing of the two
The two instructions produce identical results in practice

questions.explanation: A disposition instruction can be satisfied by an honest-sounding compliment; a content instruction requires the model to actually produce a specific deliverable — a real counter-argument — that validating the plan doesn't fulfill.

questions.from: This module — When you should not be asking a model at all
questions.prompt: Why is repeatedly rephrasing a personal decision until the answer feels right described as building an echo chamber rather than getting a second opinion?

options.label: It combines a no-ground-truth judgment call with the freedom to iterate toward a preferred framing, letting someone unconsciously fish for validation while experiencing it as independent advice
The model has no stake in the outcome, which makes every answer it gives fully independent regardless of how it was asked
This isn't actually a real risk — personal decisions get the same quality of answer as any factual question

questions.explanation: Having no stake in the outcome doesn't make the model's answer independent of framing — the sycophancy pull still tracks whatever premise the latest phrasing contains, and repeated rephrasing lets that compound into a self-built echo chamber.

questions.from: Previous module — Bias in Practice
questions.prompt: Why can a phrase like “unstable income” or “employment gaps” function as biased output even though it never names a protected characteristic?

options.label: It acts as a proxy — it correlates strongly with specific real-world groups, and the model reproduces that correlation from the hiring and lending text it trained on
It can't function as biased output — bias requires explicitly naming a protected category
The model deliberately chose vague language to hide discriminatory intent

questions.explanation: From Bias in Practice: proxy phrases don't need to name a category to correlate strongly with one in practice — the model reproduces the correlation because it exists, unremarked, in the real screening and lending language it learned the genre from.

questions.from: Previous module — Bias in Practice
questions.prompt: Why isn't a single run of each version of a controlled bias test enough to conclude a real pattern exists?

options.label: A single run can't distinguish a real, attributable difference from ordinary run-to-run generation variance — repetition is what shows whether the pattern holds up
A single run is actually sufficient proof, as long as the two versions changed exactly one variable
Models always produce identical output on every run of the same prompt

questions.explanation: From Bias in Practice: models aren't perfectly deterministic, so only a pattern that holds up across repeats counts as real evidence rather than a one-off.

questions.from: Previous module — Bias in Practice
questions.prompt: Why does an unconstrained “write me a productivity routine” prompt reliably default to assuming stable, consistent daily energy?

options.label: The majority of productivity content the model trained on is written by and for people with stable energy, and that majority pattern becomes the silent default absent any stated constraint
It's technically impossible for a model to generate a routine that accounts for variable energy
The model actively refuses to consider health conditions in general requests

questions.explanation: From Bias in Practice: an unconstrained request gets filled with the majority pattern in the relevant training content, which skews toward stable-energy assumptions.

questions.from: Previous module — Bias in Practice
questions.prompt: Why can't a longer list of “don't assume X” instructions ever fully solve default-driven bias?

options.label: Prompting only overrides the defaults you already know to name — the ones you don't think to flag, often because they fit your own situation, stay in effect regardless of list length
It actually does fully solve the problem once the list is specific and long enough
Prompt instructions of this kind have no measurable effect on model output

questions.explanation: From Bias in Practice: a checklist can only protect against what's already on it — testing is the tool that surfaces a default the requester didn't already know to name.

questions.from: Older module — Fabrication
questions.prompt: A fabricated case citation is best understood, mechanically, as:

options.label: The model completing a highly regular shape with specifics it isn't actually retrieving from anywhere
A deliberate lie the model tells when asked a leading question
A memory error where a real citation got garbled in transit

questions.explanation: From Fabrication: there's no honesty step or memory-retrieval step being failed — it's the same plausible-shape generation process regardless of whether the citation turns out to be real.

questions.from: Older module — Verifying Efficiently
questions.prompt: Why is asking the same model “are you sure?” in the same conversation a weak verification step?

options.label: It's answered by the same process with no new access to an external source — a claim checked against itself rather than against anything outside it
Models are specifically programmed to always answer “yes” to that exact question
It's actually a strong check, as long as it's asked twice in a row

questions.explanation: From Verifying Efficiently: the follow-up is generated the same way the original claim was — a plausible continuation, not a lookup against something genuinely new.

title: Arithmetic, counting and the things it's oddly bad at
description: It's not that the model doesn't know how many letters are in a word — the representation it operates on doesn't expose letters the way it exposes words, which makes counting a genuinely different, less reliable operation than writing fluently.

learningObjectives.text: Explain, mechanistically, why letter-counting and large arithmetic fail in ways that seem surprising given the model's fluency elsewhere
Predict which numeric and counting tasks are reliable versus risky based on the underlying mechanism

contentSections.title: How many r's in “strawberry”

contentSections.body: For a real stretch of time, asked “how many r's are in the word strawberry,” a range of widely-used chat models confidently answered “2” — not 3 — a question a six-year-old could answer correctly just by looking carefully at the letters. The same models could write a fluent, accurate paragraph about strawberry cultivation in the same conversation.

contentSections.question: Why would a model that can write fluently and accurately about botany get a simple letter-count in a common word wrong?
contentSections.answer: Because of how text actually gets processed before generation: the input isn't handled as a sequence of individual letters the way a person reading visually scans them — it's broken into tokens, often multi-letter chunks, and “strawberry” may be represented as a small number of sub-word pieces rather than nine separate letters in order. Counting a specific letter means reconstructing letter-level information from a representation that doesn't natively expose it — a genuinely different and less reliable operation than producing fluent prose, which works directly with the patterns tokens are good at capturing.
contentSections.hint: Think back to how text gets chopped up before a model ever processes it — is it letter by letter, or in larger chunks?

contentSections.body:
This is a structural mismatch, not a knowledge gap. Text fed into a language model is first broken into tokens — chunks that are often whole common words or common word-fragments, not individual characters. “Strawberry” might become a small number of sub-word pieces rather than a sequence of nine visible letters the way a person reading the word does. Fluent writing about strawberries draws on word- and phrase-level patterns, which tokens represent well. Counting a specific letter inside a word requires reconstructing letter-level detail that the token representation doesn't hand over directly — an indirect, unreliable operation layered on top of a representation built for something else entirely.

The same mismatch explains why multi-digit arithmetic is unreliable in a way that surprises people who've watched a model write flawless code or explain calculus. The model isn't retrieving “4,827 × 6,193” as a memorized fact, and it isn't doing digit-by-digit column multiplication the way a person taught long multiplication does — it's predicting plausible-looking digits based on patterns in how numbers and calculations typically appear in text. That works remarkably well for small, extremely common calculations that show up constantly in training data, and breaks down for larger or less common ones, with nothing in the model's tone signaling the shift from reliable to unreliable.

contentSections.scenario: You give a general-purpose chat model, with no calculator or code tool, one hundred multiplication problems where both numbers have four or more digits (like 4,827 × 6,193) and ask it to compute the exact answer directly.
contentSections.question: Out of 100, roughly how many would you expect it to get exactly, digit-for-digit, correct?
contentSections.explanation: The exact number varies by model and by how the model happens to have been trained, but the pattern holds broadly: without an attached calculation tool, large multi-digit multiplication is genuinely unreliable — closer to a plausible guess than a computed answer — because the model is predicting digit patterns rather than performing the actual arithmetic algorithm. This is exactly why many products now attach a real calculator or code-execution tool behind the scenes for numeric tasks, rather than relying on the base model's raw digit prediction.

contentSections.body: It's not that it doesn't know how many letters are in a word — the representation it operates on doesn't expose letters the way it exposes words, so counting them is a genuinely different, less reliable operation than writing fluently about them.

contentSections.title: What's actually safe versus actually risky, numerically

contentSections.body: “What's 12 times 4?” gets answered instantly and correctly, every time. “What's 4,827 times 6,193?” is far more likely to come back wrong — confidently, with no hedge distinguishing the two, and often not even close.

contentSections.scenario: A handful of numeric tasks: (1) “What's 7 times 8?” (2) “What's 84,392 divided by 17?” (3) “How many words are in this 40-word paragraph?” (4) “What's the square root of 144?”
contentSections.question: Based on the actual mechanism — not intuition about what “feels hard” — which of these are reliable, and which are risky?

options.label: (1) and (4) are reliable — small, extremely common calculations essentially memorized as patterns; (2) and (3) are risky — large arithmetic and precise counting both require reconstructing information the model's representation doesn't directly expose
All four are equally reliable, since they're all “simple math” a calculator could do instantly
(2) is the only risky one — division is inherently harder for a model than multiplication or counting

feedback.correct-split: Right — “7 times 8” and “the square root of 144” are both small, extremely common values that show up constantly in training data and are essentially memorized as patterns, not computed. “84,392 divided by 17” is a large, uncommon calculation, and counting words in a paragraph runs into the same token-versus-character mismatch as counting letters — the model isn't natively working with a clean, countable unit list the way a person scanning the text is.
feedback.all-reliable: Task difficulty for a human calculator (or a real calculator) doesn't track task reliability for a language model — the model's reliability depends on how common and small the specific values are in training data, and on whether the task requires reconstructing information its token representation doesn't directly expose, not on how “simple” the operation looks.
feedback.division-only: Counting words in a paragraph has the same structural issue as counting letters — both require reconstructing a precise unit-by-unit count from a token representation that doesn't naturally expose individual units the way visual scanning does. It's not that division specifically is the hard operation; scale and commonness matter more than which operation is being performed.

contentSections.concept: Reliability tracks two specific mechanisms, not difficulty as a person would judge it: whether a value is small and common enough to be essentially memorized as a pattern, and whether the task requires reconstructing letter- or unit-level detail the token representation doesn't directly expose.

contentSections.body: Small, common calculations are reliable because they're essentially memorized patterns, not because the model is “doing math” — the reliability drops off exactly where the pattern stops being common, with no warning in the model's tone.

title: Current events, and knowing what it can't know
description: A training cutoff isn't a wall the model announces hitting — asking about the day after cutoff can produce the same confident, plausible-shaped answer as asking about anything else it's unsure of, and a search tool moves that problem without removing it.

learningObjectives.text: Explain why a training cutoff produces confident wrongness rather than an obvious, self-flagged gap
Distinguish what a live-search or browsing tool actually fixes about the cutoff problem from what it doesn't

contentSections.title: Asked about something that happened after it stopped learning

contentSections.body: Asked about the outcome of a recent event that happened after its training cutoff, a model without live search either declines to answer — or, worse, answers confidently with something plausible-sounding based on how similar situations have generally gone before, in a tone completely indistinguishable from a real, grounded answer.

contentSections.scenario: Without live browsing access, a model is asked what happened in a specific recent event that occurred after its training data ends. Rather than clearly saying “I don't have information about that,” it produces a specific, confident-sounding account.
contentSections.question: Why would a model without live access sometimes answer this kind of question instead of clearly declining?

options.label: This is the same fabrication mechanism from earlier in this phase — there's no built-in signal separating “this is genuinely in my training data” from “this fits the shape of things I've seen enough to complete,” so an unanswerable current-events question gets the same shape-completion treatment as an obscure historical one
The model has a specific setting that makes it guess deliberately whenever it detects a knowledge gap
This only happens with obscure or unimportant events, never with major recent news

feedback.same-fabrication-mechanism: Right — this connects directly back to the fabrication module: there's no internal flag distinguishing “I actually have this” from “I can complete a plausible-sounding version of this.” A question about the day after cutoff gets the exact same treatment as any other question the model can produce a fluent, confident-sounding answer to without a real basis.
feedback.deliberate-guessing-setting: There's no such setting — this isn't a strategic choice being made, it's the same generation process (most plausible continuation) that produces every other answer, applied to a question where there's no real basis this time.
feedback.obscure-only: This can happen with major, high-profile events too if they occurred after the specific model's cutoff — recency relative to that cutoff is what matters, not how important the event is.

contentSections.mechanism: A training cutoff isn't a hard stop the model can sense and announce — it's simply the point after which there's no more training data, and the same fluent, plausible-completion process that handles everything else handles a post-cutoff question too, without a reliable internal signal marking the difference.

contentSections.body: This is worth connecting explicitly to the fabrication module, because it's the same underlying gap wearing a different label. A “training cutoff” sounds like it should behave like hitting a wall — a clear boundary the model can sense and flag. It doesn't work that way. The model has no separate, reliable internal check that says “this specific fact falls after my training data ends, therefore I should express uncertainty.” It just generates the most plausible continuation given the question, the same as always — and a plausible continuation to “what happened in this recent event” can be produced whether or not the model actually has grounded information about it. That means the practical warning sign isn't a change in tone. It's simply knowing, from context, that a question concerns something recent enough to plausibly fall after the specific model's training cutoff — and treating that category of question with the same default suspicion as any other high fabrication-risk pattern from earlier in this phase.
A training cutoff isn't a wall the model announces hitting — asking about the day after cutoff can produce the same confident, plausible-shaped answer as asking about anything else it's unsure of.

contentSections.title: Live tools change this, partially

contentSections.body: Someone assumes that because their AI assistant can now “search the web,” the cutoff problem is fully solved — then watches it cite a real, current, correctly-dated article and still get a specific detail from that same article wrong in its summary.

contentSections.scenario: Deciding what a live-search or browsing tool actually fixes about the training-cutoff problem, and what it doesn't.
contentSections.question: Which of these does attaching a search tool genuinely fix?

items.label: Access to information published after the base model's training cutoff
Whether the model correctly summarizes and represents what it retrieves
Whether the retrieved source itself is accurate or reliable
Whether the specific claim you actually care about needs independent checking

explanation.access-to-recent: This is the genuine fix — a search or browsing tool can retrieve pages published well after the base model finished training, which base generation alone cannot do.
explanation.correct-summarizing: Retrieval doesn't guarantee correct summarization — the same underlying model still has to represent what it found accurately, and it can still misstate, drop, or subtly distort a detail from a source it genuinely retrieved.
explanation.source-reliability: A search tool can retrieve an unreliable or wrong source just as easily as a reliable one — retrieval finds pages that exist, not pages that are correct.
explanation.specific-claim-check: This never goes away regardless of tooling — verification module 2's core lesson (checking against a source, not memory) still applies, now aimed at the retrieved source instead of the model's raw memory.

contentSections.synthesis: A live-search tool genuinely fixes access to recent information — it doesn't fix whether the model summarizes what it finds correctly, whether the source it found is itself reliable, or whether the specific claim you care about still needs an independent check.

contentSections.body: A search tool moves the cutoff problem, it doesn't remove it — now you're trusting retrieval and summarization instead of memory, and both still need checking.

title: Tasks where being usually right is worthless
description: An accuracy percentage that sounds great in the abstract can be worthless in practice — the question isn't “how often is it right,” it's “what happens the time it's wrong, and who's checking.”

learningObjectives.text: Evaluate whether a task's error tolerance makes 'usually right' acceptable or actively dangerous
Identify categories of task where a single wrong output has outsized cost regardless of the overall hit rate

contentSections.title: 95% right is a great score and a terrible outcome

contentSections.body: A tool that's right 95% of the time sounds excellent framed as an accuracy statistic. Framed as “used for medication-dosing calculations, wrong 1 time in 20, with no independent check before the dose is administered” — the exact same number reads as reckless. Nothing about the number changed. Everything about what it means did.

contentSections.scenario: For a task like unsupervised medication-dose calculation or an unreviewed legal-deadline calculation — genuinely high-stakes, hard-to-reverse tasks — think about what error rate would actually be low enough to skip an independent human check entirely.
contentSections.question: What error rate, out of 100 uses, would need to be true before skipping an independent check became reasonable for a task like this?
contentSections.explanation: There effectively isn't a nonzero error rate that makes skipping the check reasonable for tasks with irreversible or safety-critical consequences — because this phase's own fabrication and verification modules already established that no prompting technique or model improvement reaches exactly zero. Any task that genuinely can't tolerate a nonzero error rate needs a human check built into the process structurally, regardless of how good the track record looks; a better-performing model changes how often the check catches something, not whether the check is needed.

contentSections.body: This connects directly to the stakes framework from Verifying Efficiently: the tasks where “usually right” is worthless are exactly the highest tier of that framework — irreversible, affecting someone other than the requester, reaching far — and the honest response to landing in that tier isn't a better-performing model or a more careful prompt. It's structurally requiring an independent human check regardless of the track record, because the entire point of the earlier module's stakes lens was that verification effort should scale with what being wrong costs, and “usually right” describes an average, while the cost of an error is paid on the specific instance that goes wrong, not spread evenly across the average. A task with catastrophic single-instance cost doesn't get safer as the average accuracy number improves — it gets safer when a structural check exists that doesn't depend on the average holding on this particular instance.

contentSections.code: Internal note at a small clinic considering an AI-drafted dosage-adjustment suggestion tool: “The model is highly accurate — internal testing shows it's correct in about 97% of cases, which is a strong result, so we're comfortable rolling it out.”
contentSections.question: What's the actual flaw in using a 97% accuracy figure this way?

options.label: 97% accuracy still means roughly 1 in 33 suggestions is wrong, and for a task where a wrong dosage suggestion can cause real harm, the decision to roll out shouldn't be based on the average accuracy number at all — it should be based on whether a structural, independent check exists for every single instance regardless of the average
97% isn't actually a high number for this kind of tool, so the flaw is just that the accuracy is too low
There's no flaw — a 97% accuracy figure from internal testing is a sufficient basis for rollout on any task

feedback.average-vs-instance: Right — this is the core distinction: the decision conflates a strong-sounding average with safety on any specific instance. A dosage tool that's right 97% of the time is still wrong roughly 1 time in 33, and the cost of that specific wrong instance is what matters, not how good the average looks in a summary report.
feedback.number-too-low: The problem isn't that 97% specifically is too low a bar and some higher number (99%, 99.9%) would fix it — for a task with genuinely irreversible, safety-critical consequences, this reasoning pattern is broken at any accuracy level below a mathematically impossible 100%, which is exactly the point: no achievable accuracy number makes the structural check optional.
feedback.no-flaw: A strong average accuracy figure is exactly the kind of reassuring statistic that should trigger more scrutiny for a high-stakes task, not less — this is the same shape as a fabrication that sounds professionally confident: the surface impressiveness doesn't map onto whether it's safe to skip independent verification.

contentSections.flawExplanation: The note treats a summary statistic about average performance as though it answered the actual question, which is what happens on the specific instance where the tool is wrong — and for a task like unsupervised dosage suggestions, that specific-instance cost is what should be driving the decision, not the average.

contentSections.body: An accuracy percentage that sounds great in the abstract can be worthless in practice — the question isn't “how often is it right,” it's “what happens the time it's wrong, and who's checking.”

contentSections.title: Recognising this kind of task before you're mid-decision

contentSections.body: A small clinic considers letting an AI tool draft dosage-adjustment suggestions to speed up a nurse's workflow, reasoning that the nurse will “just double check it.” Six months in, under real time pressure and after a long streak of correct suggestions building trust, that double-check has quietly become a glance.

contentSections.code: Safety plan for a high-stakes AI-assisted task: “The nurse will review every AI-generated dosage suggestion before it's used, so we don't need any additional structural safeguard.”
contentSections.question: What's the actual flaw in relying on “the human will double-check it” as the entire safety plan?

options.label: It depends on a check happening every single time under real conditions — time pressure, fatigue, and a long streak of correct outputs building false trust — rather than making the check structurally unskippable regardless of those conditions
Nurses are not qualified to review AI-generated dosage suggestions at all, regardless of how the process is set up
This is actually a sound plan, and no further safeguard is needed once a human reviewer is assigned

feedback.unenforced-vigilance: Right — this is the same failure pattern as Verifying Efficiently's routine-without-escalation-rule problem, applied here: individual vigilance predictably erodes exactly under the conditions — deadline pressure, fatigue, a long run of correct outputs — where the check is most needed, and a plan that depends entirely on vigilance holding up every single time isn't a structural safeguard.
feedback.qualification: The scenario doesn't hinge on the nurse's qualifications — a qualified, capable reviewer is still subject to the same erosion of vigilance under repeated exposure and time pressure that any person is. The flaw is in the plan's structure, not the reviewer's competence.
feedback.sound-plan: This is exactly the plan the lesson is warning against — 'the human will double-check it' sounds sufficient in the abstract and predictably erodes in practice, which is the whole reason it needs a structural backstop rather than resting entirely on an individual's sustained vigilance.

contentSections.flawExplanation: A safety plan that depends on a person remembering to check carefully every time, indefinitely, under whatever conditions actually arise, is a hope rather than a safeguard — and hope erodes exactly under the deadline pressure and accumulated trust that make the check most necessary.

contentSections.body: The practical lesson isn't “never use AI assistance for high-stakes tasks” — it's recognizing the category before you're mid-decision and building a structural safeguard into the process itself: a second reviewer who's actually required, not just expected; a hard block that prevents the output from being used until a specific check is logged; a random audit of a sample even when nothing seems wrong. None of that depends on any individual's vigilance holding up on a bad day, which is precisely the condition a purely human safeguard is most likely to fail under.
“The human will double-check it” is not a safeguard for a high-stakes task — it's a hope, and hope erodes exactly under the deadline pressure that makes the check most needed.

title: Judgement calls that are not yours to delegate
description: Well-reasoned-sounding text doesn't transfer accountability — you're still the one who has to answer for the decision, whether or not a model helped phrase the reasoning.

learningObjectives.text: Distinguish a task a model can legitimately assist with from a judgment call that using a model to make it inappropriately offloads responsibility
Evaluate a real scenario for whether delegating the actual decision, not just the supporting research or drafting, is appropriate

contentSections.title: Drafting the email versus deciding to let someone go

contentSections.body: A manager, weighing whether to terminate an underperforming employee, feeds an AI assistant the documented performance issues and asks: “should I let them go?” A different manager, facing the same situation, asks the assistant to organize the documented performance issues into a clear, factual summary for a meeting she's going to have regardless of what she ultimately decides.

contentSections.scenario: Two requests about the same underlying situation: (A) “Should I let them go — yes or no?” (B) “Organize these documented performance notes into a clear, factual timeline I can use in the meeting.”
contentSections.question: Which of these is a legitimate use of a model, and which offloads a judgment call that should stay with an accountable human?

options.label: (B) is legitimate — it asks the model to support and structure information the manager still has to weigh; (A) offloads the actual, consequential judgment call about another person's employment onto a process with no accountability and no full context on the human situation
Both are equally fine — either way, the manager is the one who reads the output and acts on it
Both are equally risky — any AI involvement in an employment decision is inappropriate, including drafting or organizing

feedback.b-legit-a-offload: Right — this is the actual line the lesson is drawing: (B) keeps the model in a support role, organizing real, checkable information the manager still has to interpret and weigh. (A) asks the model to make the actual call, on a decision with real consequences for another person's livelihood, where the model has no accountability for the outcome and no access to the full human context a decision like this actually requires.
feedback.both-fine: Reading the output and technically acting on it doesn't make the two requests equivalent — (A) invites the manager to treat the model's yes/no as though it were a real recommendation carrying some independent weight, which is a different psychological and practical position than using the model purely to organize facts she's already weighing herself.
feedback.both-risky: This overcorrects — the lesson isn't arguing against any AI involvement in employment-adjacent tasks, only against asking the model to make the actual consequential judgment call. Drafting, organizing, and summarizing documented facts is a legitimate and useful role that doesn't offload the decision itself.

contentSections.concept: The line isn't about the topic (employment decisions are always off-limits) — it's about whether the model is being asked to organize information the accountable person still weighs, or to make the actual call.

contentSections.body: The model can organize the facts you're weighing. It shouldn't be asked to weigh them for you, on a decision that carries real consequences for someone else and stays yours to answer for.

contentSections.title: Why “it gave good reasons” doesn't fix this

contentSections.body: After the model answers “should I let them go?” with what reads as a well-reasoned yes — citing the documented pattern, the missed deadlines, the prior warnings — the manager feels better about a decision she now experiences as validated by an outside, seemingly objective source. Nothing about who is accountable if the decision turns out to be wrong or unfair has changed.

contentSections.question: Does a well-reasoned-sounding answer to a delegated judgment call make it more legitimate to have delegated it in the first place?
contentSections.answer: No. Coherent, well-organized reasoning is something the model produces fluently regardless of whether the underlying judgment is actually sound — the same shape-versus-substance gap that runs through fabrication (a fluent citation isn't evidence it's real) and sycophancy (a fluent counter-argument isn't evidence it's specific) shows up here too: fluent reasoning isn't evidence the judgment itself was the model's to make. More importantly, reasoning quality doesn't transfer accountability — the manager remains the person who has to answer for the outcome, with or without an AI-generated justification attached to it.
contentSections.hint: Compare this to the fabrication module's core point about fluency: does sounding confident and well-reasoned ever, on its own, tell you something is actually correct?

contentSections.body: This closes the loop on a theme that's run through this entire phase: fluency and soundness are not the same property, and a model producing coherent-sounding text is not evidence that the underlying content — a citation, a counter-argument, or here, a judgment call — has the substance its polish implies. What makes a category of decision genuinely inappropriate to delegate isn't that a model can't produce plausible-sounding reasoning for it; it's that the reasoning, however coherent, doesn't carry any of the accountability the decision actually requires. The categories worth naming explicitly: decisions with legal or employment consequences for another person, medical or safety judgment calls specific to a real patient, and ethical decisions you personally have to live with and answer for. In all three, a legitimate role for a model looks like organizing information, surfacing considerations you might have missed, and drafting communication — not making the call.
Well-reasoned-sounding text doesn't transfer accountability — you're still the one who has to answer for the decision, whether or not a model helped phrase the reasoning.

title: Keeping your own picture current
description: A documented limit is a snapshot, not a permanent fact — re-test the ones your own work actually depends on, instead of either freezing them forever or re-litigating everything constantly.

learningObjectives.text: Evaluate whether a previously-learned limitation still holds, given that model capabilities change over time
Construct a personal habit for periodically re-testing a load-bearing assumption about what a model can and can't do

contentSections.title: The limit that used to be true

contentSections.body: Someone learned, a while back, that AI models were unreliable at basic arithmetic and counting, and still routinely double-checks every single number a model produces — including small, common calculations a current model would get right nearly every time — a habit that made complete sense when it formed and now costs more effort than it protects.

contentSections.question: Was it a mistake to have originally learned “don't trust its arithmetic” as a rule?
contentSections.answer: No — it wasn't a mistake to learn something true when it was true. The mistake is treating any specific “it can't do X” as a permanent fact rather than a snapshot that needs periodic re-checking, because model capabilities are actively changing: yesterday's real limitation can become today's non-issue, and — just as often — a new limitation nobody has documented yet can quietly appear in exactly the tasks that used to be safe.
contentSections.hint: Separate the question of whether the belief was correct when formed from the question of whether it's still correct now.

contentSections.body: This creates a genuine double bind, and it's worth naming honestly rather than resolving it with a slogan. A limits list is genuinely useful — this whole module exists because knowing what not to trust saves real effort and prevents real harm. And a limits list genuinely goes stale, in both directions at once: some limits close as models and tools improve at specific tasks they used to fail, and new limitations appear in tasks that used to be reliable, as models change in ways that aren't always documented anywhere the average user would see. The two tempting resolutions are both wrong. “Distrust everything forever, to be safe” burns exactly the kind of misapplied effort Verifying Efficiently spent an entire module warning against. “Trust it completely because it's clearly improved” is the overcorrection — assuming general improvement means a specific, previously-documented failure mode is gone, without ever checking. The actual resolution is a habit: periodically re-testing a handful of your own real, load-bearing assumptions against the current model you're actually using, on your own real tasks — not running forever on secondhand folklore about what “AI can't do,” frozen at whatever moment you first heard it.
A documented limit is a snapshot, not a permanent fact — re-test the ones your own work depends on, instead of running forever on what used to be true.

contentSections.title: Building the habit, not just the document

contentSections.body: Someone building their own limits document — the module's upcoming lab — worries it'll be outdated the moment they finish writing it. That worry is correct, and it's not a reason not to write it; it's a reason to build the document around a re-test habit rather than around a belief that it's finished.

contentSections.intro: Assemble a simple, sustainable personal habit for keeping a limits list current, field by field.

fields.prompt: Which limits should actually get re-tested?
options: The specific limits your own real, recurring work actually depends on knowing accurately — not every limit anyone has ever documented
Every limit ever documented by anyone, re-tested on a fixed schedule regardless of relevance to your work
fields.correctValue: The specific limits your own real, recurring work actually depends on knowing accurately — not every limit anyone has ever documented
fields.feedback: Re-testing everything is its own version of the over-checking trap from Verifying Efficiently — the habit only survives if it's scoped to the handful of assumptions your actual work genuinely leans on.

fields.prompt: How often should a load-bearing assumption actually get re-checked?
options: On a cadence tied to how much a wrong assumption there would actually cost you, similar to the stakes-based thinking from Verifying Efficiently — not a fixed calendar date picked arbitrarily
Never — once documented, a limit should be treated as permanently settled
fields.correctValue: On a cadence tied to how much a wrong assumption there would actually cost you, similar to the stakes-based thinking from Verifying Efficiently — not a fixed calendar date picked arbitrarily
fields.feedback: The same stakes-proportional logic from the verification module applies here — a load-bearing assumption behind a high-stakes recurring task deserves more frequent re-checking than a minor convenience assumption.

fields.prompt: What, besides a calendar date, should prompt a re-check?
options: A specific update to the model or tool you're using, or a task failing in a way that contradicts a documented limit
Nothing else — only a fixed schedule should ever trigger a re-check
fields.correctValue: A specific update to the model or tool you're using, or a task failing in a way that contradicts a documented limit
fields.feedback: A version change or a surprising real-world failure is a more useful, timely trigger than a fixed date — it catches the exact moment a limit is most likely to have shifted.

fields.prompt: What's explicitly not worth constantly re-testing?
options: Low-stakes assumptions where being wrong costs almost nothing to notice and correct in the moment
Nothing — every assumption, however minor, deserves the same re-testing rigor
fields.correctValue: Low-stakes assumptions where being wrong costs almost nothing to notice and correct in the moment
fields.feedback: This is the other half of the stakes logic — spending re-test effort on a low-cost assumption is the same misallocation Verifying Efficiently warned against, just applied to maintaining a limits document instead of checking a single output.

contentSections.synthesis: A sustainable re-test habit is scoped to the handful of assumptions your real work actually leans on, checked on a cadence proportional to what being wrong would cost, triggered by real signals (a version change, a surprising failure) as much as by a calendar, and deliberately skips re-litigating low-stakes assumptions that don't need it.

contentSections.body: The goal isn't a document that's permanently correct — it's a habit of updating a few load-bearing assumptions on a cadence, instead of either freezing them forever or re-litigating everything constantly.

title: Practice — Judge Eight Tasks as Suitable or Not
description: Eight drills applying the token/counting mismatch, the cutoff-versus-search distinction, the average-versus-instance stakes trap, and the delegate-versus-decide line to new tasks. No new concepts.

learningObjectives.text: Judge whether a given task falls inside or outside a model's genuine reliability, given the specific mechanism behind the limit
Identify whether a task requires a structural safeguard rather than reliance on individual vigilance

contentSections.title: Eight tasks, eight judgment calls

contentSections.body: Same drill, eight times, with the task changed: a real request or scenario, and the question of whether it falls inside a genuine limit from this module — and why, specifically, not just a general sense of “that seems risky.”
If a drill needed a hint, that's the pattern to watch for in your own AI use this week — not a reason to redo the set.

title: Lab — Write Your Own Limits Document
description: Sort your own real AI-assisted tasks by risk tier, test your current assumptions about the highest-risk ones instead of relying on secondhand folklore, and write a personal document stating what you will and won't delegate — plus a re-test cadence to keep it current.

learningObjectives.text: Sort real, personally relevant tasks by risk tier using the module's stakes framework
Test current, specific limits rather than relying on outdated or secondhand assumptions

contentSections.title: A document built to be updated, not just written once

contentSections.body: List the real tasks you actually use, or would consider using, an AI assistant for — not a hypothetical inventory, the actual ones from your actual week. Some of them are low-stakes and forgiving. At least one or two probably aren't, and you may be running on an assumption about them that's never actually been tested against the tool you're currently using.

contentSections.title: A personal list of what you will and won't use a model for, with reasons
contentSections.brief: List your real, current AI-assisted tasks and sort them by what a wrong, undetected output would actually cost — not by how the task feels. For the higher-risk tasks specifically, test your current actual assumption about the model's reliability rather than relying on something you read or learned a while ago. Write the final document: what you will delegate outright, what you'll delegate only with a structural safeguard (name the safeguard specifically), what you won't delegate at all and why, and a stated cadence for re-testing the load-bearing assumptions behind it.
contentSections.deliverable: A written document listing your real tasks sorted by risk tier with a one-line reason for each tier placement; for each higher-risk task, what you actually tested and what you found (not just what you assumed); a clear statement of what you will delegate outright, what needs a named structural safeguard, and what stays entirely with you; and a stated re-test cadence with at least one non-calendar trigger.

stages.title: List and sort your real tasks by risk tier
stages.instructions: List the actual tasks you use or would use an AI assistant for. For each, ask what a wrong, undetected output would actually cost — using the irreversibility, who's-affected, and reach factors from Verifying Efficiently — and sort into low / needs-a-safeguard / don't-delegate tiers.
stages.checkpoint: You have a real task list, sorted into three tiers, each with a one-line reason tied to actual cost rather than a gut feeling.

stages.title: Test your current assumptions on the higher-risk tasks
stages.instructions: For each task in the higher tiers, state the specific assumption you're currently running on about what the model can or can't reliably do for it. Actually test at least two of these assumptions against the tool you use now — don't rely on something you read or learned previously without checking.
stages.checkpoint: You have at least two documented tests of real assumptions, with what you actually found, not just what you expected to find.

stages.title: Write the final document and a re-test cadence
stages.instructions: Write the document: what you'll delegate outright, what needs a named structural safeguard (not "I'll be careful"), and what stays entirely yours to decide. State a re-test cadence for the load-bearing assumptions, including at least one non-calendar trigger (a tool update, a surprising failure).
stages.checkpoint: You have a finished document with all three delegation tiers stated, at least one named structural safeguard, and a stated re-test cadence with a non-calendar trigger.

rubric.criterion: Tasks are sorted by actual cost of a wrong, undetected output, not by intuition
rubric.meets: Each tier placement has a one-line reason referencing irreversibility, who's affected, or reach — not just a general impression of riskiness.

rubric.criterion: At least two current assumptions were actually tested, not assumed
rubric.meets: The document shows what was actually run and what was found, including if the result surprised the learner or contradicted an older belief.

rubric.criterion: Structural safeguards, where named, are actually structural
rubric.meets: A named safeguard is something unskippable by design (a required second reviewer, a hard block) rather than a restated intention to be careful.

rubric.criterion: At least one task is explicitly marked as not to be delegated, with a specific reason
rubric.meets: The document names a real task that stays fully with the learner and states why — an irreversible cost, a judgment call that isn't theirs to offload, or both.

rubric.criterion: A concrete re-test cadence is stated, including a non-calendar trigger
rubric.meets: The cadence names both a rough time interval and at least one event (a version update, a surprising failure) that should also prompt a re-check.

contentSections.body: This document is going to be wrong about something within a year, on purpose — the point isn't that it's permanently correct, it's that you've named the specific things worth checking again, and when.

title: Checkpoint — What It Cannot Do
description: Ten questions: four from this module, four reaching back to Agreement and Flattery, two reaching further back — one each from Fabrication and Verifying Efficiently.

learningObjectives.text: Retrieve the counting/token mismatch, the cutoff-versus-search distinction, the average-versus-instance stakes trap, and the delegate-versus-decide line without looking them up

contentSections.title: What stuck
Checkpoint — What It Cannot Do
contentSections.framing: Four questions from this module, four reaching back one module to Agreement and Flattery, two reaching further back — one each from Fabrication and Verifying Efficiently.

questions.from: This module — Arithmetic, counting and the things it's oddly bad at
questions.prompt: Why does a model reliably get simple letter- or word-counting wrong in ways that seem surprising given its fluency elsewhere?

options.label: Text is processed as tokens — often multi-letter chunks — rather than individual characters, so counting a specific letter requires reconstructing detail the representation doesn't directly expose
The model refuses to engage carefully with counting tasks because it finds them uninteresting
Counting is impossible for any language model under any circumstances, including with external tools

questions.explanation: This is a structural mismatch between the token representation and letter-level detail, not a knowledge gap or a refusal — fluent writing draws on patterns tokens capture well, while counting requires reconstructing something the representation doesn't natively expose.

questions.from: This module — Current events, and knowing what it can't know
questions.prompt: What does attaching a live-search tool genuinely fix about the training-cutoff problem, and what does it not fix?

options.label: It fixes access to information published after the cutoff; it doesn't fix whether the model correctly summarizes what it retrieves, or whether the retrieved source itself is reliable
It fixes everything — a search-enabled model needs no further verification on any current-events question
It doesn't help at all — search tools have no effect on the cutoff problem

questions.explanation: A search tool solves the genuine access problem but leaves summarization accuracy, source reliability, and the need for independent verification of specific claims exactly as they were.

questions.from: This module — Tasks where being usually right is worthless
questions.prompt: Why can a 97% accuracy figure be the wrong basis for deciding whether a high-stakes task needs an independent human check?

options.label: It describes an average across many cases, while the cost of an error is paid entirely on the specific instance that's wrong — a strong average doesn't make any individual instance safer to skip checking
97% is simply too low, and the same reasoning would be fine at a higher number like 99.9%
Accuracy figures are always a sufficient basis for this kind of decision

questions.explanation: For a genuinely irreversible or safety-critical task, the average accuracy figure doesn't tell you which instance will be the wrong one — the structural check is needed regardless of how good the average looks, since no achievable accuracy figure below 100% removes the risk on a specific instance.

questions.from: This module — Judgement calls that are not yours to delegate
questions.prompt: Why doesn't a well-reasoned-sounding AI answer to a delegated judgment call make delegating it more legitimate?

options.label: Fluent, coherent reasoning is something a model produces regardless of whether the underlying judgment is sound, and it doesn't transfer accountability for the outcome away from the person who has to answer for it
It does make it more legitimate — well-reasoned output is exactly what should determine whether delegation was appropriate
Models are incapable of producing reasoning that sounds coherent for judgment calls
